META.subject: Physics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 2.1 (12 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Physics
UNIT.content:
• Rectilinear propagation of waves
• Reflection of waves (laws of reflection, ripple tank and light)
• Refraction of waves (change in speed and direction, Snell's law idea)
• Diffraction of waves (effect of wavelength and gap size)
• Interference of waves (constructive and destructive, path difference)
• Standing (stationary) waves on strings and in air columns
• Doppler effect (moving source and observer)
• Applications of wave properties in day-to-day life (radio and FM communication, mobile phone networks, sonar, ultrasound scans)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) describe the rectilinear propagation of waves using ray and wavefront diagrams,
b) investigate reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference of waves using ripple tanks, strings, light and sound,
c) explain the formation of standing waves and the Doppler effect using the wave equation v = fλ,
d) apply the properties of waves to explain everyday phenomena such as echoes, radio and FM reception, and the changing pitch of passing sirens,
e) appreciate the application of wave properties in communication, medicine and technology in Kenya.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learners analyse wave evidence from simulations and experiments to explain why waves bend around obstacles, cancel out or change pitch.
• Communication and collaboration: learners work in groups to run ripple tank and string investigations and present findings and models to the class.
• Digital literacy: learners use PhET simulations (Wave Interference, Bending Light, Geometric Optics, Standing Waves on a String), videos and Khan Academy resources to gather evidence.
• Learning to learn: learners revisit the Driving Question Board and revise their models as new evidence emerges.
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: learners take care of apparatus and fulfil assigned roles in group investigations.
• Unity: learners cooperate to collect and pool data and build shared class models.
• Respect: learners listen to and value the explanations and predictions of peers.
• Integrity: learners report observations honestly, even when results differ from predictions.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners generate questions about the matatu sound mystery for the Driving Question Board.
• Developing and using models: learners draw and revise wavefront, ray and standing-wave models across the unit.
• Planning and carrying out investigations: learners use ripple tanks, slinky springs and strings to test reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference.
• Analysing and interpreting data: learners analyse frequency, wavelength and speed data using v = fλ.
• Using mathematics and computational thinking: learners calculate wave speed, frequency and wavelength, and simulate waves digitally.
• Constructing explanations: learners explain the anchoring phenomenon using evidence.
• Engaging in argument from evidence: learners defend or revise predictions in class discussions.
• Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information: learners read and present on FM radio, sonar and ultrasound.
UNIT.pcis:
• Safety and Security Education: learners handle electrical ripple tank equipment safely and learn about the dangers of loud noise to hearing.
• Environmental Education: learners link noise pollution in towns like Nairobi and Mombasa to sound wave behaviour.
• Health Education: learners relate ultrasound scans and hearing protection to wave properties.
• Digital Citizenship: learners use online simulations and videos responsibly.
UNIT.careers:
• Telecommunications engineer: designs mobile phone and FM radio networks for Safaricom, Airtel and radio stations across Kenya.
• Radiographer or sonographer: uses ultrasound waves for medical imaging at hospitals such as Kenyatta National Hospital.
• Meteorologist: uses radar and Doppler effect to track weather at the Kenya Meteorological Department.
• Audio engineer or acoustician: designs sound systems and halls, for example at the Kenya National Theatre.
• Marine and fisheries technologist: uses sonar to locate fish in Lake Victoria and the Indian Ocean.
• Physics teacher or researcher: teaches and investigates wave phenomena.
UNIT.focus: This unit uses one everyday puzzle, hearing a matatu's music around a corner while its pitch changes as it passes, to drive the study of wave properties. Learners predict, observe through simulations and hands-on investigations, explain with the wave model, and keep revising a class model and Driving Question Board across 12 lessons. The unit moves from rectilinear propagation through reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference and standing waves to the Doppler effect and real-world applications such as FM radio.
UNIT.phenomenon: On a busy Nairobi street, a matatu blasting music is parked behind a building. Students standing around the corner cannot see the matatu, but they can clearly hear the music, even though a torch beam from the matatu would be blocked by the wall. When the matatu drives past, the pitch of its horn and music is higher as it approaches and suddenly lower as it moves away, even though the driver does not change the sound. On the same trip, the FM radio inside the matatu fades and crackles at certain spots near the Ngong Hills and comes in clearly again a few metres on. Students find this puzzling: why do sound waves seem to bend around obstacles when light does not, why does the pitch change for a moving source, and why does the signal strength vary from place to place if the radio station never changes?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• An echo returns from a rock face at Hell's Gate or a hall wall after you shout, but not in an open field.
• A straw looks bent in a glass of water, and ripples slow down and change direction when they pass from deep to shallow water in a basin.
• A plucked guitar string or nyatiti string produces a clear musical note only at certain lengths and tensions (standing waves).
• An ambulance siren on Mombasa Road sounds higher-pitched when approaching and lower when leaving (Doppler effect).
• Two speakers playing the same note in a hall create loud spots and quiet spots (interference).
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media?
2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Introduce the matatu phenomenon; students predict, record initial models and generate questions for the Driving Question Board (DQB).
Lesson 2: Rectilinear propagation of waves; use the PhET Geometric Optics simulation and ripple tank wavefronts to show how waves travel in straight lines in a uniform medium.
Lesson 3: Reflection of waves; investigate the laws of reflection with ripple tanks, plane mirrors and echoes, and revise the model.
Lesson 4: Reflection applications; explain echoes, sonar fish-finding on Lake Victoria and the effect of hall design on sound, and add to the DQB.
Lesson 5: Refraction of waves; investigate speed and direction change using ripple tank depth changes, PhET Bending Light and YouTube demonstrations.
Lesson 6: Refraction calculations and applications; use v = fλ to explain why wavelength changes but frequency does not, and explain the bent straw.
Lesson 7: Diffraction of waves; use PhET Wave Interference and the ripple tank to see how gap size and wavelength affect bending, and begin explaining why sound turns the corner but light does not.
Lesson 8: Diffraction and the corner puzzle; compare sound and light wavelengths, then revise the model to explain the matatu music heard around the building.
Lesson 9: Interference of waves; investigate constructive and destructive interference using two ripple sources and speakers, and explain the loud and quiet spots and fading FM radio.
Lesson 10: Standing waves; use the PhET Standing Waves on a String simulation and a slinky or guitar string to relate string length, tension, nodes and antinodes to musical notes.
Lesson 11: Doppler effect; use a YouTube demonstration, Khan Academy and a classroom moving-buzzer activity to explain the changing pitch of the matatu horn and the ambulance siren.
Lesson 12: Applications and synthesis; explore FM modulation and ultrasound, then finalise the class model, revisit the DQB and explain the whole matatu phenomenon in a written and oral presentation.

LESSONS.title: The Matatu Mystery: Launching the Phenomenon
LESSONS.aresKeywords: wave, disturbance, energy, sound, pitch, frequency, wavelength, FM radio, signal, obstacle, Driving Question Board, initial model

slo.purpose: To launch the matatu phenomenon so that learners observe three puzzles (sound heard around a corner, pitch change of a moving horn, and fading FM radio near the Ngong Hills), record their own initial ideas, and ask testable questions that will drive the whole sub-strand.
slo.knowledge: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one point to another without transferring matter. Learners observe that sound is heard around a 4.0 m opening while a torch beam is blocked, that a matatu horn of true frequency 400 Hz is heard at 418 Hz while approaching and 383 Hz while receding, and that a 100 MHz FM station fades at certain spots near the Ngong Hills. These values are only observed in this lesson, not calculated.
slo.skills: Making predictions from prior knowledge of sound and light (NGSS SEP: Asking Questions and Defining Problems). Developing an initial model with drawings and words (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models). Observing and recording evidence from a demonstration (NGSS SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations). Turning puzzling observations into testable questions. Communicating ideas in pairs and to the class (Communication and collaboration).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday phenomena on Kenyan roads. Respect for peers' diverse ideas and open-mindedness when ideas differ (Respect). Responsibility in contributing roles within a group. Appreciation of the importance of Physics in day-to-day life.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson. It introduces the anchoring phenomenon, surfaces learners' prior ideas, starts the class model with three parts (A: corner/diffraction, B: pitch/Doppler, C: signal fading/interference) and opens the Driving Question Board (DQB). Later lessons return to the DQB questions: Lesson 2 addresses why the torch beam is blocked by the wall, and later lessons progressively revise Models A, B and C.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep the buzzer-on-a-string swing in a clear space with learners at arm's length from the swinger. Keep the volume of speakers and the horn recording at a safe level and not close to ears. During any outdoor corner demonstration, stay on the school compound away from roads and vehicles. Use a torch carefully and never shine it into anyone's eyes.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau opens by describing a real trip: Baraka, a matatu driver on the Nairobi-Ngong route, keeps his horn steady at 400 Hz and his radio tuned to one 100 MHz FM station. Wanjiru and Otieno stand around the corner of a building on a busy Nairobi street. They cannot see the parked matatu hiding behind a concrete wall, yet they hear its music clearly, while a torch beam from the matatu would be blocked. When Baraka drives past at a constant 15 m/s (54 km/h), the horn sounds like 418 Hz while approaching and suddenly 383 Hz while moving away, though Baraka never changes it. Near the Ngong Hills, the radio fades and crackles at certain spots and returns a few metres later, though the station never changes. Learners predict individually, observe a demonstration (a buzzer on a string, a slinky pulse, and a recorded matatu horn and music, with a torch and wall comparison), build a first explanation of what a wave is (a disturbance that carries energy), generate questions for the DQB, and draw an initial three-part class model (A, B, C). Nothing is explained fully in this lesson; the goal is productive puzzlement and testable questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners hear the story of Baraka's matatu, Wanjiru and Otieno at the corner, and the Ngong Hills radio. Working silently for 4 minutes in their notebooks, each learner writes predictions and reasons for three prompts: (A) Wanjiru and Otieno cannot see the matatu behind the concrete wall. Will they hear the music? Would a torch beam from the matatu reach them? Why? (B) When the matatu drives past with its horn steady, will the pitch they hear stay the same, rise, or fall? (C) The FM radio is tuned to one station but fades near the Ngong Hills. What might cause this? They then do a Think-Pair-Share, comparing predictions with a partner and marking where they agree or disagree.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the phenomenon aloud slowly and say: "Before I tell you anything, I want your honest first ideas. There are no wrong predictions today; wrong ideas are useful to us." Use a clear voice and show a sketch of the street, wall, matatu and the two students on the board. Ask: "Who has ever heard a matatu or boda boda they could not see?" Take 3 hands. After the silent writing, say "Turn to your partner and share your reason, not just your answer." Circulate to at least 6 pairs and listen for words such as 'sound bends', 'sound is louder', 'light goes straight', 'frequency', 'signal'. Then cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share one prediction each, using WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before calling and saying "Take your time, I will wait." Record predictions on the board in three columns A, B, C without judging them. Ask: "Who thought something different? What was your reasoning?" Do not give any explanation.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with prediction and reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain). Writing predictions with reasons makes prior ideas visible to the learner and the teacher, and creates a personal stake in the evidence later, so learners notice when evidence confirms or challenges their thinking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that 90% of learners have written a prediction with a reason for all three prompts A, B and C. Look for indicators of prior ideas: learners who say sound 'goes round' versus those who say it 'reflects off other buildings'; learners who say the horn 'changes by itself' or 'gets louder' versus those who link pitch to speed; learners who blame 'weak signal', 'hills' or 'weather' for fading. Tally on the board the number of learners who predict that sound is heard, that the pitch rises/falls/stays the same, and who attribute fading to the hills. Note learners who confuse pitch and loudness for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 with assigned roles (Reader, Recorder, Materials manager, Reporter), learners rotate through three short stations of about 6 minutes each, recording observations and drawings in a table of 'What we saw/heard' and 'What puzzles us'. Station 1 (Corner): a speaker or phone plays music from behind a classroom partition or a wall corner (or learners go outside the classroom door to the corner of the building), while a torch is shone from the same hidden spot. Learners record what they hear and what they see. The observed outcome: the music is heard around the corner but the torch light is blocked. Learners note the 4.0 m street opening in the story is similar to the width of a corridor gap. Station 2 (Pitch): learners listen to a recording of the matatu horn (true frequency 400 Hz) passing by; Mr Kamau tells them a phone app shows 418 Hz heard on approach and 383 Hz heard on moving away, while Baraka keeps the horn at 400 Hz. They also swing a small buzzer on a string in a safe circle and listen from the side to hear the pitch rise and fall. They record only what they hear and the values given, with no calculations. Station 3 (Signal): learners listen to a pre-recorded FM radio clip from the 100 MHz station, with the signal fading, crackling, and returning, played as the matatu moves near the Ngong Hills, and they look at a simple diagram showing the hillside and radio tower. They note the fading spots are metres apart (about 1.5 m, given as an observed value only). Then, with a slinky stretched on the floor between two learners, they send a single push-pull pulse and watch what moves along the slinky and what does not.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the stations, say: "Today you are scientists, not answer-finders. Your job is to observe carefully and write exactly what you see and hear, without explaining yet." Show how to fill the observation table with one worked example row. At Station 1, ask: "What can Wanjiru and Otieno hear? What can they see? What did the torch do?" Wait 10 seconds before accepting answers. At Station 2, say: "The driver never touched the horn. What do you notice about the pitch? Write 'higher' or 'lower' and the numbers 418 Hz and 383 Hz, and ask yourselves what could be changing." Clarify that pitch is what we hear related to frequency and loudness is amplitude, and that they are not the same. At Station 3, ask: "The station never changes. What did the signal do?" At the slinky, ask: "When the pulse reached the other end, did the coils travel to your partner? What moved?" Circulate and cold-call 2 groups at each station to read one observation aloud. Use the timer, rotating groups every 6 minutes. After rotation, hold a whole-class debrief: "What was the same across all three puzzles?" Wait 15 seconds and take 4 responses. Do not explain diffraction, Doppler or interference; if learners ask, say: "Great question. Put it on a sticky note for our Driving Question Board."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation with Notice and Wonder. Separating 'What we saw/heard' from 'What puzzles us' trains learners to distinguish evidence from inference. Using multiple contrasting observations (sound versus light, rising versus falling pitch, strong versus fading signal) from one phenomenon helps learners see patterns that need explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect each group's observation table. Success indicators: records that the music is heard but the torch beam is blocked; records both 418 Hz (approaching) and 383 Hz (receding) against the true 400 Hz; records that the radio signal fades at certain spots though the station is fixed; observations are written separately from explanations. At the slinky, listen for learners saying 'the pulse moved but the coils only moved back and forth'. Mark groups that mix explanations into observations for prompts. Aim for at least 8 of 10 groups to have complete tables.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their predictions and discuss with their group: Which predictions matched what we observed? Which did not? Using the slinky and the buzzer, they construct a first explanation of 'What is a wave?' They complete the sentence frame: 'A wave is a ______ that carries ______ from ______ to ______ without carrying ______.' Then they connect the idea to the phenomenon: the horn vibrates the air, the vibration travels as a sound wave to Wanjiru and Otieno's ears; the radio signal is also a wave that travels from the transmitter to the matatu radio. Each group writes a 3-sentence 'best idea so far' for each of puzzles A, B and C and marks each with a confidence level (1-3) and one thing they would need to find out. They share in a gallery walk, adding one sticky-note comment (a question or a 'we think the same because...') to two other groups' posters.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at your predictions. Put a tick where the evidence agrees and a question mark where you are not sure." Then ask: "When Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music, what is travelling from the matatu to their ears? Is it air, or something else?" Use WAIT TIME of 15 seconds and cold-call 3 learners. Use the slinky to model: push-pull one end and ask, "What moved along the slinky, and what stayed roughly in place?" Guide learners to the idea that a wave is a disturbance carrying energy, not matter, noting that the music is heard but no air is blown from the matatu to Wanjiru. Say: "This is our starting definition. We will test it throughout the unit." Clarify that this lesson only introduces that waves carry energy, and later lessons will examine how they behave. Circulate during group writing and ask each group: "What would you need to see or measure to convince a sceptical friend?" During the gallery walk, set a 6-minute timer and ensure each learner writes at least one sticky note. Cold-call 3 learners to read one note that challenged their thinking. Avoid giving the real explanations of diffraction, Doppler effect, or interference; respond to such ideas with "Interesting, let's park it on the DQB and test it."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) draft with a gallery walk. Learners state a tentative claim for each puzzle, cite evidence from the stations, and give reasoning with a confidence rating. The gallery walk exposes competing ideas and builds a need for more evidence, reinforcing that science explanations are revised as evidence grows.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for and record whether learners can state that a wave transfers energy without transferring matter (indicator: use of the slinky pulse as evidence). Check each group poster for a claim, at least one piece of evidence from the stations, and a reasoning sentence for each of A, B and C. Look for common misconceptions: 'the horn itself changes', 'sound only travels in straight lines like light', 'the radio station is moving'. Use a quick thumbs check (up, sideways, down) on 'I can say what a wave carries', and note the number of learners with thumbs sideways or down for reteaching in Lesson 2.

framework.learnerExperience: The class gathers around a large chart or wall space headed with the driving question: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' Each learner writes 2 questions on separate sticky notes that start with 'Why', 'How' or 'What would happen if', and that could be tested. In groups they sort questions into three clusters (A: corner/sound and light, B: pitch change, C: radio fading) plus a fourth cluster 'Other / how waves are used'. They star the questions they most want to answer and rewrite at least one vague question (e.g., 'Why is sound strange?') into a testable question (e.g., 'Does a wider gap change how much sound bends round a corner?'). Examples may include: 'Does a faster matatu make a bigger pitch change?', 'Would a lower pitch bend around the wall more than a high pitch?', 'Does the radio fade at the same spots every time?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "A good scientific question is one we could test with an experiment, a measurement or a model. Let's practise." Model one rewrite on the board, turning 'Why is the pitch weird?' into 'How does the speed of the matatu change the pitch we hear?' Give 4 minutes of silent writing. Then say: "Place your notes under the heading that fits best. If it fits two, make a copy." Cold-call 4 learners to read a question aloud and explain why it belongs in its cluster, with 10 seconds of WAIT TIME beforehand. Ask: "Which question could we test in this classroom with a ripple tank, two speakers, a slinky, a guitar string or a buzzer on a string? Which needs a simulation?" Highlight links to the KICD key inquiry questions by asking: "Which of our questions are about waves meeting obstacles or different media? Which are about how waves are used in daily life?" Tell learners the DQB stays up all unit and that questions will be answered and moved to an 'answered' area with evidence. Photograph the board and keep a record. Do not answer the questions now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering. Sorting and rewriting questions into testable forms gives learners ownership of the unit, shows how their curiosity connects to the three parts of the phenomenon, and provides a visible record against which later evidence can be compared.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that every learner has contributed at least 2 questions and that at least 60% are testable (they name something that can be changed, measured or compared). Look for questions in all three clusters A, B and C and at least some linking to everyday applications of waves. Record learners who write only yes/no or purely factual questions for support in later lessons. Observe whether learners can justify cluster placement using evidence from the stations (for example, 'the torch was blocked but the music was not').

framework.learnerExperience: Each group draws an initial class-model poster in three labelled parts. Part A (corner): a top-view sketch of the street, the concrete wall, the 4.0 m opening, the hidden matatu, Wanjiru and Otieno, with arrows showing how they think sound and light travel. Part B (pitch): a sketch of the matatu approaching and then moving away at 15 m/s with the horn at 400 Hz, showing what they think happens to the sound between the horn and the listener, and labelled with the observed 418 Hz and 383 Hz. Part C (signal): a sketch of the Ngong Hills, the 100 MHz FM transmitter, and the matatu, showing how they think the signal reaches the radio and why it fades at certain spots about 1.5 m apart. Under each part they write 'What we think is happening' and 'What we still need to find out' and use a different coloured pen for each part. The class then merges group ideas into one class model on large paper, kept visible for revision in each lesson. Finally, learners complete a 3-row summary table: What we observed, What we learned, What we can explain so far.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Models are tools for thinking. They are meant to be wrong at first and better later. Draw what you think is happening, including things we cannot see, like the sound itself." Give 12 minutes for drawing. Circulate and press for mechanism with prompts such as: "What is travelling from the horn to the ear in your picture?", "Why did you draw the light and the sound differently?", "Where in your model does the pitch change happen?" Do not correct drawings; instead ask "What evidence from the stations supports that?" Cold-call 3 groups to explain one part of their model, with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question, and invite two other groups to ask one question. Build the class model on the wall, using one colour for ideas that most groups share and another for ideas that are disputed. Close with: "Today we have a first model and a board full of questions. Next lesson, we start with the torch and the wall: why does the beam stop, and how do we draw how waves travel?" Have learners fill the summary table as an exit ticket.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial (progressive) modelling. Drawing a first model with 'what we think' and 'what we need to find out' makes hidden mechanisms visible, allows later lessons to revise a single class model in three parts (A, B, C), and shows learners that explanations improve as evidence grows.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use the group posters and exit tickets. Indicators of success: each model includes all three parts A, B and C; Part A shows a different path or behaviour for sound and light; Part B uses the values 418 Hz, 383 Hz and 400 Hz correctly as observations and does not blame the horn; Part C includes the transmitter, the hillside and the matatu radio; each part has a 'still need to find out' note; the exit-ticket table separates observations from tentative explanations. Record at least 80% of groups meeting 4 of these 5 indicators; note common initial ideas to compare with later models.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which of the three puzzles (the corner, the pitch change, the fading radio) generated the most curiosity and the most initial ideas, and why? Did learners separate observations from explanations in their tables? Which prior ideas (for example 'sound bends because it is stronger', 'the horn changes', 'the hills block the signal') will need to be revisited in later lessons? Were the questions on the DQB testable enough, and which learners need support in writing them? Did I resist explaining diffraction, Doppler effect and interference, and did I give enough WAIT TIME? What adjustments are needed so that every learner, including those who spoke less, can contribute to the class model in Lesson 2?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Write what you observed about the three puzzles: the music heard around the corner while the torch beam was blocked by the wall, the matatu horn (true frequency 400 Hz) heard at 418 Hz while approaching and 383 Hz while receding at 15 m/s, and the 100 MHz FM radio fading at certain spots near the Ngong Hills though the station never changes.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Write what you learned today: a wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter (as shown by the slinky pulse and the sound from the matatu horn), and good scientific questions are testable.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Write what you can explain so far, and what you cannot yet explain: give your best first idea for each of Parts A (corner), B (pitch) and C (fading signal) in your model, and list one question from the Driving Question Board that you want answered next.

LESSONS.title: Waves Travel in Straight Lines: Rays, Wavefronts and the Blocked Torch Beam
LESSONS.aresKeywords: rectilinear propagation, ray, wavefront, uniform medium, ripple tank, shadow, wavelength, frequency, wave equation v = fλ

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how waves travel in a uniform medium, so they can explain why the torch beam from the matatu is blocked by the wall and what 'straight-line travel' means for light and for water waves. This gives the first piece of evidence for Model Part A (corner/diffraction).
slo.knowledge: Rectilinear propagation: waves travel in straight lines in a uniform medium. A wavefront is a line joining points in phase. Rays are drawn perpendicular to wavefronts and show the direction of travel. Light in air travels at 3.0x10^8 m/s. In the ripple tank at 10 Hz in deep water, wavelength λ = 3.0 cm and v = 0.30 m/s, which agrees with the wave equation v = fλ (10 x 0.030 = 0.30 m/s).
slo.skills: Predicting and sketching rays; observing wavefronts in a ripple tank and a simulation; using the PhET Geometric Optics simulation to test light travel past an obstacle; applying the wave equation v = fλ; developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2); analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4); constructing explanations using evidence (SEP 6).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity and open-mindedness when comparing sound and light; teamwork and respect for diverse ideas (Communication and collaboration); responsibility when handling the ripple tank and lamp; appreciation of how physics explains everyday Nairobi experiences.
slo.keyInquiry: How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? (Focus: how do waves travel when nothing is in the way, so we can later tell what changes at an obstacle?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners saw three puzzles and asked why the torch beam is blocked by the wall while the music is heard around the corner. Lesson 2 establishes the baseline: in a uniform medium waves travel in straight lines. Learners can then explain the blocked torch beam and the sharp shadow. This sets up reflection (Lesson 3), refraction (Lessons 5 and 6) and diffraction (Lessons 7 and 8), where the straight-line rule is bent. Lesson 2 does NOT explain why sound turns the corner; that comes later.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep electrical equipment (ripple tank lamp and vibrator) away from spilled water; wipe up spills immediately and put the tank on a stable bench. Do not look directly into the lamp or torch. Hold the torch steady, never shine it at faces. Learners hold the tank edges only when it is switched off. Keep bags off the floor around the tank.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau opens by recalling the Lesson 1 question: why does a torch beam from the parked matatu stop at the wall, even though Wanjiru and Otieno can hear the music around the corner? Learners predict and sketch how light and water waves travel. They observe a ripple tank with a 10 Hz vibrator producing straight wavefronts (deep water, λ = 3.0 cm, v = 0.30 m/s) and use the PhET Geometric Optics simulation and a torch behind a card with a slit to see rays travelling in straight lines and casting sharp shadows. In the Explain phase they define wavefront and ray, check v = fλ with the ripple data, and explain the sharp shadow behind the wall for light. They add new questions to the DQB (why does sound NOT make a sharp shadow?) and build Model Part A, v1: waves travel in straight lines in a uniform medium, so light is blocked by the wall, but the sound puzzle remains open.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four and recall Lesson 1: Wanjiru and Otieno hear Baraka's matatu music around the building, but a torch beam from the matatu would be blocked by the 4.0 m-wide street's concrete wall. Each learner draws on a card (1) the path of a torch beam leaving the matatu and meeting the wall, and (2) the path of water ripples spreading from a point and passing a straight barrier. Beside each sketch they write one sentence beginning 'I predict the waves travel...' and one reason. Groups compare and agree on one group prediction to share.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 puzzles. Say: 'Last lesson we asked why the torch beam is blocked by the wall. Today we find out how light and other waves travel when nothing is in the way. Draw what you think the path looks like.' Give 3 minutes. Walk round and photograph 3 contrasting sketches (straight, curved, spreading) without commenting on correctness. Say: 'Do not rub out; wrong ideas help us.' Cold-call 3 groups to explain their sketch. After each, WAIT TIME 10 seconds, then ask: 'Who has a different path? What made you choose it?' Record predictions on the board under 'Our predictions'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Compare (Elicit prior ideas): committing a drawn prediction in public makes learners aware of their current thinking, so later evidence can be tested against it and ideas that change can be seen as progress.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) how many sketches show a straight path versus a curved one; (b) whether learners use words such as 'ray', 'beam' or 'wave'; (c) whether learners assume sound and light behave the same way (note, do not correct). Tally on a clipboard: aim to identify 3 key alternative ideas to revisit in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Station 1 (Ripple tank, teacher-led demonstration with learner helpers): A vibrator at 10 Hz makes a straight dipper bar produce plane wavefronts in deep water. Learners view the pattern on the white screen, measure the distance across 5 wavefronts with a ruler on the screen (5 wavelengths = 15 cm, so λ = 3.0 cm) and record the 10 Hz frequency. They calculate v = fλ = 10 x 0.030 = 0.30 m/s. A point dipper is then used to show circular wavefronts, and learners note that the wavefronts spread but each part of a wave still moves outward in a straight line along the radius. Station 2 (PhET Geometric Optics simulation or torch demonstration): Learners shine a torch through a slit in a card toward a screen, then place a wooden block (the 'wall') in the path. They sketch the rays, the lit region and the shadow. In the simulation they place an object and a light source, and test whether the rays can ever curve around the object. Light travels at 3.0x10^8 m/s, so it covers the 4.0 m street opening in about 1.3x10^-8 s, which seems instant. Learners record in a table: wave type, what they saw, path shape (straight/curved), shadow sharp or fuzzy.
framework.teacherMoves: Set up the ripple tank before class and test the 10 Hz vibrator. Say: 'Watch the wavefronts. What do you notice about their shape and direction?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds before taking answers. Ask a learner helper to measure across 5 wavefronts and say: 'Why do we measure 5 wavelengths instead of 1?' (reduces reading error). Cold-call 4 learners to report the measured λ and the calculated v. At Station 2 say: 'Move the block slowly. Where does the shadow begin and end? Is the edge sharp?' Circulate; ask: 'If the beam bent, where would the shadow edge be?' Ask a group to hold a string taut from the torch to the screen edge to check the straight line. Remind learners of safety rules for water and lamps. Say: 'Record what you SEE, not what you think should happen.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation with data table and Analysing and Interpreting Data (SEP 4): recording the same features (path shape, shadow edge, measured λ) for both water and light lets learners spot the common pattern across different waves rather than treating each demonstration as separate.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each learner's table records (a) 10 Hz, λ = 3.0 cm, v = 0.30 m/s; (b) straight-line rays and a sharp shadow for light; (c) the observation that no light enters the shadow region. Observable indicators: learners using a ruler or string to test straightness; correct unit conversion of 3.0 cm to 0.030 m. Note groups that report a 'fuzzy edge' due to a large torch and ask them how to improve the experiment (narrower slit, darker room).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their tables to build a class definition of wavefront (a line joining points in phase, such as all the crests) and ray (a line perpendicular to the wavefronts that shows the direction of travel). They label a diagram of the ripple-tank plane waves with 3 wavefronts spaced 3.0 cm apart and rays drawn at right angles. They state the rule 'In a uniform medium, waves travel in straight lines (rectilinear propagation)' and explain what uniform means (same material, same speed throughout, e.g. air of the same temperature, water of the same depth). Then in pairs they draw a ray diagram for the matatu torch beam hitting the wall from Lesson 1: the rays go straight, the wall blocks them, and a shadow forms behind it where Wanjiru and Otieno stand. They write a 3-sentence claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) explanation of why the torch beam is blocked. They end by writing one question: 'If waves travel in straight lines, why can we still hear the music?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your data. What do the ripple wavefronts and the torch rays have in common?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds, then ask pairs to share with a partner before cold-calling 4 pairs. Introduce the terms: 'A wavefront joins points that are in step, like all the crests. A ray is an arrow showing direction and always meets the wavefronts at 90 degrees.' Draw one example on the board and have learners correct a deliberately wrong version where a ray is drawn along a wavefront. Prompt: 'Why does the shadow have a sharp edge?' Press for evidence: 'What did you see that shows that?' Present the CER frame: 'Claim: ... Evidence: ... Reasoning: ...'. Then challenge: 'The music reaches Wanjiru and Otieno but the torch beam does not. Does today's rule explain the music?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Say clearly: 'Today's rule works for light in a uniform medium. We will test sound and corners in later lessons. Hold that question.' Do not explain diffraction now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (SEP 6) with Developing and Using Models (SEP 2): connecting ripple-tank and torch evidence to a general rule through a labelled wavefront-and-ray diagram. The explicit 'does it explain the music?' prompt creates a productive gap that motivates the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that CER statements include: Claim (light travels in straight lines so the wall blocks it), Evidence (sharp shadow, straight string line, plane wavefronts in ripple tank), Reasoning (rectilinear propagation in a uniform medium). Indicators of understanding: rays drawn at 90 degrees to wavefronts; correct use of 'uniform medium'. Common errors to listen for: 'light is faster so it can't bend', 'sound is not a wave'. Collect 6 exit notes with the question 'Name one thing a ray tells us.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the driving question: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' Groups write new questions on sticky notes, such as 'Why does sound not make a sharp shadow like light?', 'Do sound waves travel in straight lines too?', 'What happens if the medium changes?', 'What happens at the edge of the wall?'. They post notes under three headings matching the three model parts: A (corner/diffraction), B (pitch/Doppler), C (signal fading/interference). They also mark any Lesson 1 questions now answered (e.g. 'Why is the torch beam blocked?') with a green tick and a note, 'Answered in Lesson 2: light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which Lesson 1 question can we now answer with evidence?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Invite 2 learners to move the sticky note and add the evidence. Say: 'Write one new question that today's evidence made you wonder about. Put your name on it.' Cold-call 5 learners to read their questions aloud and ask the class to decide which heading each belongs under. Ask: 'Which question needs a different kind of evidence, such as sound?' Group related questions with a marker. Do not answer unanswered questions; say: 'We will return to these as our evidence grows.' Photograph the board for the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a Question Tracking Tool: moving questions between 'open' and 'answered' with cited evidence makes learning progress visible and gives learners ownership of the investigation sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count the number of new questions (aim for at least one per group) and check that they link to evidence from this lesson. Indicators: learners cite the ripple tank or torch shadow when justifying a green tick; questions mention sound, edges or bending rather than only restating the driving question. Note whether any learners cluster questions under the correct model part.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the class model for the matatu phenomenon, which has three parts. They add the first evidence-based entries to Part A (corner/diffraction), version 1: a diagram showing the matatu hidden behind the building wall, the 4.0 m-wide street opening, Wanjiru and Otieno around the corner, and straight rays from a torch stopped by the wall, with a shadow region behind it. They label 'Light: straight rays, blocked by wall, sharp shadow (rectilinear propagation in uniform air, 3.0x10^8 m/s)' and 'Water waves in ripple tank: plane wavefronts, 10 Hz, λ = 3.0 cm, v = 0.30 m/s'. For sound they draw a dotted question mark path from the matatu to the students and write 'We can hear it. Straight-line rule alone does not explain this yet.' Parts B and C are left as 'Not yet investigated.' Finally each learner completes the summary table: what we observed, what we learned, what we can explain.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use only evidence we have collected. Draw what the straight-line rule predicts for the torch beam, then show where sound does something different.' Provide a large model template on chart paper. Give 5 minutes for groups to draw, then a gallery walk of 3 minutes. Cold-call 3 groups to explain one part of their model. WAIT TIME 10 seconds after each explanation before inviting questions. Ask: 'What does your model explain? What does it leave unexplained?' Press: 'What do you think the sound waves do at the edge of the wall?' Accept ideas as hypotheses and record them on a 'To test' list. Close: 'Next lesson we investigate what happens when waves hit a surface and bounce back.' Collect the summary tables.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (SEP 2): the class model is built in versions, with each lesson adding evidence-based elements and explicitly marking gaps, so learners see how a scientific model grows and where it still fails.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that Part A v1 has straight rays blocked by the wall, a shadow region, correct figures (3.0x10^8 m/s; 10 Hz; λ = 3.0 cm; v = 0.30 m/s; 4.0 m opening) and an honest question mark for sound. Indicators of success: learners distinguish what the model explains (torch beam blocked) from what it does not (music around the corner). Listen for learners using the terms 'ray', 'wavefront' and 'uniform medium' correctly. Review summary tables to identify those who need support with the wave equation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Reflect on the following after the lesson: (1) Did learners separate what they predicted from what they observed in the ripple tank and torch activities? Which prediction was most common, and did learners revise it with evidence? (2) Could learners explain why the torch beam is blocked using the words ray, wavefront and uniform medium? Which learners still thought light 'bends a little' or that sound and light behave identically? (3) How well did the ripple-tank measurement of 5 wavelengths work, and did learners correctly convert 3.0 cm to 0.030 m in v = fλ? (4) Were the DQB questions linked to evidence, and did any learners already ask about edges or bending that you can build on in Lessons 7 and 8? (5) Did you avoid explaining diffraction too early, and how did learners respond to leaving the sound question open? (6) What adjustments to equipment (darker room, narrower slit, offline simulation) or grouping would improve participation, especially for learners who rarely speak?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the ripple tank at 10 Hz in deep water we saw straight, evenly spaced plane wavefronts with wavelength 3.0 cm, and we calculated v = 0.30 m/s. A torch beam through a slit travelled in a straight line, and a block in its path made a dark shadow with a sharp edge.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: In a uniform medium waves travel in straight lines (rectilinear propagation). A wavefront joins points in phase, and a ray is drawn at 90 degrees to the wavefronts to show direction. Light travels at 3.0x10^8 m/s in air and obeys this rule.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain why a torch beam from the matatu is blocked by the concrete wall: the light rays travel straight and cannot pass through or around the wall, so a shadow forms where Wanjiru and Otieno stand. We cannot yet explain why the music is heard around the corner, and that question stays on the Driving Question Board.

LESSONS.title: Bouncing Back: Reflection and the Laws of Reflection
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; adjust to school timetable)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: reflection, law of reflection, incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, wavefront, plane mirror, ripple tank, barrier, echo

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how waves bounce off surfaces. They use plane mirrors and ripple tank barriers to discover that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and they use this to explain how an echo returns from a wall. This prepares them to explain how the Ngong Hills reflect the FM signal (Part C of the class model).
slo.knowledge: State the law of reflection: the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r, with angles measured from the normal, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. Describe reflection of ripples at a straight barrier (wavelength 3.0 cm and frequency 10 Hz do not change on reflection). Explain that an echo is a sound wave reflected from a wall, using the echo test: a student 85 m from a wall hears the echo after 0.50 s.
slo.skills: Predicting, observing and measuring angles with a protractor; drawing ray diagrams with a normal; identifying patterns in data (i vs r); using wavefronts and rays to represent reflection; developing and using models (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models); analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP); constructing explanations.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how waves behave at boundaries; careful, honest measurement; collaboration in groups and respect for others' ideas; appreciation of how physics explains everyday experiences such as echoes and mirrors in Nairobi.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 raised three puzzles about the matatu: sound around the corner, the pitch change, and the fading FM signal. Lesson 2 showed that waves travel in straight lines in a uniform medium, using rays and wavefronts. Lesson 3 asks what happens when a wave hits a surface. It gives learners the law of reflection, which they will need later for the Ngong Hills reflected signal (Lesson 9, Part C), reflection at fixed ends of strings (Lesson 10), and echoes and sonar (Lesson 4). Part A (corner/diffraction) and Part B (Doppler) are not changed in this lesson, but learners record that reflection alone does not explain the bending of sound around a corner.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep water in the ripple tank away from electrical sockets and wipe up spills immediately to prevent slipping. Keep the vibrator and lamp cables off the wet floor. For the echo test, clap in an open school field away from roads, with an adult supervising. Handle mirrors carefully to avoid broken glass, and never shine a torch or reflected sunlight into anyone's eyes.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau returns to the Nairobi street scene. Wanjiru and Otieno hear the music, but could the sound be reaching them by bouncing off a wall across the street? Learners predict how ripples and light behave at a barrier, then investigate with a ripple tank (10 Hz, wavelength 3.0 cm), plane mirrors and a ray box or torch. They measure angles of incidence and reflection and discover the law of reflection. They then analyse the echo test (student 85 m from a wall, echo after 0.50 s) as evidence that sound reflects like other waves. Finally they add reflection to the class model and to the Driving Question Board (DQB), noting what reflection does and does not explain about the matatu phenomenon.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four with the picture of the Nairobi street and the matatu behind the building. Mr Kamau asks: 'Could the music reach Wanjiru and Otieno by bouncing off the building across the street? What happens when a wave hits a wall?' Individually, each learner sketches in their notebook (a) a ripple wavefront hitting a straight barrier at an angle and (b) a torch ray hitting a plane mirror at an angle, drawing where they think the wave goes afterwards. They then compare with a partner and add a one-sentence prediction: 'I think the angle the wave leaves at compared with the angle it arrives at will be ______ because ______.' This links Lesson 2 rays and wavefronts to the Lesson 1 puzzle.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'In Lesson 2 we learned that waves travel in straight lines. What do you think happens when a straight-moving wave hits a wall? Draw it before we test anything.' Circulate and photograph or note 3 different predictions (e.g. wave goes straight into the wall, bounces back along the same path, bounces off at an equal angle). Give 3 minutes of silent drawing, then WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after asking: 'Who can tell us what angle their wave leaves at?' Cold-call 4 learners from different groups and ask them to hold up sketches; do not say who is correct. Record the competing predictions on the board under a heading 'Our predictions about bouncing waves'. Remind groups that ripples are water waves, light is a wave, and sound is a wave.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Gallery of Predictions: committing to a prediction in writing creates a mental stake, so surprising or confirming evidence in the next phase is noticed and discussed. Comparing varied predictions surfaces misconceptions (for example, that waves 'stick' to the wall or bounce straight back at any angle).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check sketches for: (a) a barrier drawn as a line and a wave or ray drawn arriving at an angle; (b) any attempt to show a normal or compare angles. Tally how many of the 4 cold-called learners predict equal angles versus straight-back or other. Look for misconceptions such as 'the wave stops at the wall' or 'sound cannot bounce'. Note learners who label wavefronts or rays correctly from Lesson 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Station work (rotate every 7 minutes, three stations; groups of four with roles: measurer, recorder, drawer, reporter). STATION 1 Ripple tank: a vibrator set at 10 Hz makes straight ripples of wavelength 3.0 cm in deep water. Learners place a straight metal barrier at an angle to the wavefronts and observe the reflected ripples under the stroboscopic light or lamp image. They sketch incident and reflected wavefronts, measure wavelength before and after reflection with a ruler on the screen (still 3.0 cm), and note the frequency stays 10 Hz. STATION 2 Plane mirror: with a ray box or torch with a slit, a sheet of plain paper, a plane mirror and a protractor, they draw the mirror line, a normal at the point of incidence, shine a ray at 20°, 30°, 40°, 50° and 60° from the normal and mark the reflected ray with pins or pencil dots. They measure angle i and angle r and fill a table. They also check that the incident ray, reflected ray and normal stay flat on the paper (same plane). STATION 3 Echo evidence: learners examine data from the echo test: a student claps 85 m from a school wall and hears the echo after 0.50 s. They calculate the total distance travelled by the sound (2 x 85 = 170 m) and the speed (170/0.50 = 340 m/s), and compare with the speed of sound in air near Nairobi, 340 m/s. They discuss how this shows that sound reflects off a wall.
framework.teacherMoves: Before rotating, say: 'Your job is to collect measurements, not to guess. Measure angles from the normal, not from the mirror surface.' Demonstrate once how to draw a normal at 90° to the mirror. At Station 1 ask: 'What is happening to the wavelength and frequency after the wave hits the barrier? How do you know?' At Station 2 ask: 'Is angle i always bigger than, smaller than, or equal to angle r? Show me evidence from your table.' At Station 3 prompt: 'Why do we multiply 85 by 2?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before taking answers. Cold-call 3 groups at each station for a quick report. Move around to check that learners use the protractor correctly and measure from the normal. If time is short, run Stations 1 and 2 as a teacher demonstration and give the echo data as a worked sheet. Keep a timer visible and signal rotations.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table pattern-finding with multiple representations (wavefront sketch, ray diagram, numerical table, real-world echo measurement). Learners look for a consistent relationship between i and r across different representations, building evidence that the same rule applies to water ripples, light and sound. This links to Analysing and Interpreting Data (NGSS SEP).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (1) measure from the normal and not from the mirror surface; (2) record at least 5 pairs of i and r with values within about 2° to 3° of each other; (3) state that the wavelength stayed 3.0 cm and the frequency stayed 10 Hz after reflection; (4) correctly calculate 170 m and 340 m/s in the echo task. Use a quick checklist during rotation and note groups needing help with protractors.

framework.learnerExperience: Back in their groups, learners study their data and write a group claim in the format Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): 'When a wave reflects from a surface, the angle of incidence i ______ the angle of reflection r. Evidence: ______. Reasoning: ______.' They then redraw one ripple tank diagram with wavefronts and rays, labelling the incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle i and angle r. With Mr Kamau, the class agrees on the law of reflection: the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. Groups then apply the law to two questions: (a) A ray hits a plane mirror at 35° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection, and what is the angle between the incident and reflected rays (70°)? (b) Using the echo test, explain how a sound wave from the student reaches the wall and returns. They also discuss: 'Does reflection explain why Wanjiru and Otieno hear music around the corner, or the pitch change?' and write one sentence on what reflection can and cannot explain so far.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A claim needs evidence from your own table. Point to the numbers.' Ask: 'Why do we measure angles from the normal instead of from the mirror?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'In the ripple tank, the wavelength stayed 3.0 cm and the frequency stayed 10 Hz. What does that tell you about the wave speed using the wave equation v = fλ?' (Expected: v = 10 x 0.030 = 0.30 m/s, the same as before.) Introduce the formal wording of the law and write it on the board. Address misconceptions: a rough wall still reflects, but scatters in many directions, while a smooth mirror gives one clear reflected ray. Press the connection to the phenomenon: 'If the music bounced off a wall opposite the matatu, would that explain why we hear it around a corner at all places, or only where the reflected path reaches? What other idea do we still need?' Do not teach diffraction or the Doppler effect here; tell learners those puzzles will be investigated in later lessons. Cold-call 4 groups to share CER statements and invite respectful challenge: 'Who can add evidence or disagree politely?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Consensus Discussion: requiring learners to link a claim to measured data and to a scientific principle builds argumentation skills (NGSS SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence). The explicit 'what reflection cannot explain' question prevents over-generalising a single idea to the whole phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for CER statements that include numbers from the table (for example 'i = 40°, r = 40°'); correct labelling of the normal on diagrams; correct answers of 35° and 70° in question (a); and the idea that the echo is sound reflected from the wall with a total path of 170 m in question (b). Listen for statements that reflection alone does not explain the bending of sound around the corner or the pitch change. Note learners who still measure from the mirror surface.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the three puzzles from Lesson 1 (sound around the corner, pitch change, FM fading). Each group writes on sticky notes: (1) one question that has been partly answered by today's lesson, and (2) one new question prompted by reflection. Example questions: 'Could the radio signal reflect off the Ngong Hills?' 'If sound reflects, why can we also hear around corners with no wall opposite?' 'Does an echo change pitch?' They place notes on the board and sort them under Part A (corner), Part B (pitch), and Part C (fading signal). One learner from each group explains where their note is placed and why.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which puzzle does reflection help with, and which does it not solve yet?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 3 groups to read and place a note. Highlight questions on Part C: 'Remember the FM signal fading near the Ngong Hills. If the hillside reflects the signal, what two signals might arrive at the same spot?' Do not give the full answer; mark this question with a star for Lesson 9. Point out questions that will be answered in Lessons 4 (echoes and sonar), 7 and 8 (diffraction), 9 (interference) and 11 (Doppler effect) so learners see the road ahead. Move any answered questions to a 'Partly answered' column with a one-line note: 'Sound and other waves reflect with i = r.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question sorting: connecting new learning to the anchoring phenomenon keeps purpose visible and shows how each investigation contributes to the final explanation. Sorting questions into Parts A, B and C builds the structure of the class model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that sticky notes are specific and testable (for example 'Does the hillside reflect the FM signal?') rather than vague ('Why waves?'). Note correct placement of questions under Parts A, B and C. Observe whether at least two groups connect reflection to Part C and whether learners recognise reflection does not yet answer Part A or B.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the class model of the matatu phenomenon with three parts: A (corner/diffraction), B (pitch/Doppler), and C (signal fading/interference). In groups they add a new component called 'Reflection': a diagram of the street showing the matatu, the building and a wall opposite, with rays from the matatu hitting the opposite wall and reflecting with i = r toward Wanjiru and Otieno, and a second diagram of the Ngong Hills as a reflecting hillside sending a signal back toward the matatu radio. They label incident ray, reflected ray, normal, i and r. Under the diagram they write: 'Waves reflect from surfaces with i = r; wavelength and frequency stay the same.' They then complete the sentence stems: 'Reflection helps explain ______ but does not yet explain ______ because ______.' Each group revises their initial Lesson 1 model on a poster or in their notebooks and notes one question for Lesson 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add what we have evidence for. Do not add ideas we have not tested yet.' Ask: 'On your model, where would the reflected FM signal meet the direct signal?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Prompt: 'The matatu is moving at 15 m/s and the FM radio is tuned to a 100 MHz station that does not change. In your model, what does reflection add to Part C? What is still missing?' (Expected: a second, reflected signal arrives, but we still need superposition and interference to explain fading, which comes in Lesson 9.) Make sure learners do not claim that reflection explains the Doppler effect or sound bending around corners. Let groups display their models for a 3-minute gallery walk. Close by reading the law of reflection aloud together and previewing Lesson 4: 'How can we use the time an echo takes to find distance?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Gallery Walk: revising a shared model after each investigation shows learners how scientific explanations are built from evidence over time (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models). The gallery walk allows peer critique and comparison of diagrams.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that models show reflected rays with equal angles measured from the normal, correct labels, and a statement that wavelength (3.0 cm) and frequency (10 Hz) stay unchanged on reflection. Look for accurate limits statements such as 'reflection alone does not explain why the FM fades' or 'we still need to explain the corner and pitch change'. Note groups that incorrectly attribute pitch change or bending around the corner to reflection.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, review: Did learners measure angles from the normal rather than from the mirror surface? Which groups found i = r from their own data, and which needed support? How did the echo calculation (2 x 85 = 170 m in 0.50 s gives 340 m/s) help learners accept that sound reflects? Did any learners claim that reflection explains the corner or pitch puzzles, and how did you respond? Were the 10-15 second WAIT TIMEs used, and did cold-calling include quieter learners? Consider whether the ripple tank worked well in your school; if not, plan a demonstration or use the PhET sound or wave simulation. Note which DQB questions to carry into Lesson 4 (echoes, sonar) and Lesson 9 (the reflected FM signal near the Ngong Hills).

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed ripples (10 Hz, wavelength 3.0 cm) bouncing off a barrier, light rays bouncing off a plane mirror with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, and an echo returning after 0.50 s from a wall 85 m away.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Waves reflect from surfaces according to the law of reflection: the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r, measured from the normal, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. Reflection does not change the frequency, wavelength or speed of the wave in the same medium. An echo is a reflected sound wave.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Sound from the matatu can reach Wanjiru and Otieno by reflecting from walls, and the Ngong Hills can reflect the FM radio signal, giving a second signal that will later be used to explain the fading spots. Reflection alone does not yet explain how sound bends around the corner (Part A), why the pitch changes (Part B), or why the signal fades (Part C), so we need more evidence in later lessons.
