LESSONS.title: Echoes, Sonar and Hall Design: Putting Reflection to Work
LESSONS.aresKeywords: echo, reflection, sonar, time delay, d = vt/2, minimum echo distance, reverberation, hall acoustics, Lake Victoria, absorber

slo.purpose: Learners apply the law of reflection from Lesson 3 to sound, using the time delay of an echo to calculate distance (d = vt/2), and explain how reflected sound shapes echoes, sonar fish-finding on Lake Victoria and hall design. This is evidence for the corner puzzle: reflected sound also reaches listeners, so not all sound at the corner needs to bend.
slo.knowledge: Learners will explain an echo as sound reflected from a hard surface and heard after a time delay. They will use d = vt/2 with v = 340 m/s in air (85 m gives a 0.50 s echo) and v = 1500 m/s in water (0.040 s gives 30 m). They will show that a separate echo needs at least 0.10 s delay, so a minimum distance of 17 m. They will describe how hard surfaces, soft absorbers and surface shape affect the sound in a hall.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (timing an echo). Using mathematics and computational thinking (rearranging d = vt/2). Analysing and interpreting data. Constructing explanations. Developing and using models (adding reflection to Model Part A).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday sound, respect for others' reasoning during talk, responsibility in group roles, and appreciation of how Physics helps Kenyan fishers and builders.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 gave the law of reflection (i = r). Lesson 4 shows reflection at work: echoes, Lake Victoria sonar and halls. Learners then ask what still cannot be explained by reflection alone (why sound reaches people who cannot see the matatu, the pitch change, the fading signal), and these questions go on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Refraction (Lesson 5) follows.
slo.safetyNotes: Do the echo test outdoors, away from traffic, with learners on a marked field. Use clapping or wooden blocks only, never loud horns. Keep learners away from the wall base and from roads. Handle the stopwatch carefully. Keep sound short and moderate to protect hearing.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau reminds the class that Wanjiru and Otieno could hear the matatu music around the corner. Some sound may have bounced off walls. Learners predict how a clap bounces off a wall 85 m away and how long the echo takes. They then observe the echo test data (0.50 s at 85 m), a PhET Sound simulation of reflection and delay, and a Lake Victoria sonar scenario (0.040 s, 1500 m/s). They explain with d = vt/2, why 17 m is the minimum for a separate echo, and how hard and soft surfaces change a hall. The class adds questions to the DQB and revises Model Part A (corner) by noting that reflection is one way sound reaches around buildings, but cannot explain the pitch (B) and fading signal (C) puzzles.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners picture the matatu parked behind the building on a Nairobi street. On a prediction sheet they answer individually for 3 minutes: (1) Student claps 85 m from a wall. Will they hear a second sound? Sketch the path of the sound using the law of reflection (i = r) from Lesson 3. (2) Predict roughly how long the echo takes (choose: 0.05 s, 0.5 s, 5 s) and explain why. (3) A fisher on Lake Victoria sends a sound pulse down to the lake bed. Predict how the fisher could find the depth. They then compare in pairs and mark their confidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember Wanjiru and Otieno around the corner. Today we ask: could some of that music have bounced off walls to reach them? Before I teach anything, I want your best prediction.' Show a drawing of the clap, wall and student. Ask: 'What do you already know about echoes from the mountains near Kericho or from a gorge?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, silently, after each question. Cold-call 3 learners for predictions and 2 for reasons without saying right or wrong. Say: 'Interesting, hold on to that idea, we will test it.' Record the three time choices as a tally on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a confidence rating: committing to a prediction before evidence creates a cognitive hook, and the tally shows the class the range of ideas. Linking to the law of reflection keeps Lesson 3 in active use.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check prediction sheets for: (a) sketch with a ray hitting the wall and returning, with i = r drawn; (b) a time estimate with a reason; (c) any idea of using time to find depth. Note learners who think the echo is a different sound or that sound goes through the wall. Indicator: at least 3 of 5 sampled learners link echo to reflection.

framework.learnerExperience: Station 1 (outdoor or video evidence): Learners watch or do an echo test. A student claps 85 m from a school wall while others time the echo with a stopwatch. The class data table shows the echo returns after 0.50 s. They repeat at about 10 m and record that the echo is not heard as a separate sound. Station 2 (PhET: Sound Simulation): in groups of 4 they send sound to a barrier, change the distance, and note how the delay changes. Station 3 (Lake Victoria sonar): a data card from a fish-finder in Kisumu says: the pulse returns after 0.040 s, speed of sound in water = 1500 m/s. Learners record in a three-column table: situation, speed, time delay, and what they notice.
framework.teacherMoves: Assign roles: timer, recorder, reporter, safety monitor. Say: 'Look at the numbers, what do you notice about distance and delay?' Circulate and ask each group: 'Why does the time double the distance travelled?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before prompting. Prompt: 'Where does the sound go, and how far does it travel in total?' At the 10 m test ask: 'Why can we not separate the echo from the clap?' Cold-call 4 groups to report one observation each. Remind: use 340 m/s for sound in air and 1500 m/s in water. Keep the safety rules: no shouting near roads.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table noticing and wondering: learners record observations before explanation, separating what they see from why. Comparing three contexts (open field, simulation, lake) helps them see the same pattern in different media.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for: 'the echo came after 0.50 s', 'closer wall, shorter delay', 'the sound goes there and back'. Check that tables show 0.50 s at 85 m and 0.040 s for sonar. Indicator: 80% of groups record both times correctly and state that the delay increases with distance.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use the data to build explanations. Step 1: Total distance travelled = 2d, so speed = 2d/t, so d = vt/2. Step 2: Check the echo test: d = 340 x 0.50 / 2 = 85 m. Step 3: Sonar on Lake Victoria: d = 1500 x 0.040 / 2 = 30 m. Step 4: The ear needs about 0.10 s to separate two sounds, so the minimum distance for a separate echo = 340 x 0.10 / 2 = 17 m. Explain why the 10 m test gave no clear echo. Step 5: Hall design: in a hall, many reflections from hard walls arrive late and blur speech; curtains, carpets and ceiling panels absorb sound, reducing echo, and a curved or angled surface directs reflected sound to the audience. Learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) statement: 'The Kisumu fisher can find the depth of 30 m because...'. Then they apply to a school assembly hall in Nairobi, suggesting two changes to reduce echo.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Talk to your partner: why do we divide by 2?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to explain using the words 'there and back'. Model the calculation on the board with units, then have pairs do the sonar calculation while you circulate. Ask: 'What would happen to the delay if the lake were 60 m deep?' (0.080 s, double). Ask: 'Why does a bare concrete hall in Mombasa sound echoey but a hall with curtains does not?' Cold-call 2 pairs. Address the misconception that hard surfaces destroy sound: 'The sound is reflected, not lost.' Connect: 'Reflection can send sound around the street, but does it explain why the matatu music is still heard when we are not in its path? Partly. It does not explain the pitch change or the fading, so we need more ideas.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with worked example then transfer: learners link numerical evidence to a physical reason (sound travels there and back), then apply the same reasoning to a new context (hall design). This builds transfer of knowledge and mathematical modelling.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that CER statements include the claim (depth is 30 m), evidence (0.040 s and 1500 m/s) and reasoning (d = vt/2 because sound travels to the bottom and back). Indicator: 4 of 5 pairs calculate 30 m with units; at least 3 correctly explain why 17 m is the minimum. Note anyone who forgets to halve and re-teach with a diagram.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB with the driving question: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' On sticky notes they write (1) what today's evidence helped answer (e.g. echoes show that sound reflects from walls, so some sound can reach the corner by bouncing) and (2) new questions (e.g. 'Does reflection explain the pitch change?', 'Why does the sound bend into the 4.0 m opening even where there is no wall to bounce off?', 'Can radio waves bounce off the Ngong Hills?'). They group notes under Part A, B, C of the model.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look back at our driving question. What did we learn today that moves us forward, and what is still a mystery?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds for writing. Ask each learner to write at least 1 new question. Cold-call 4 learners to read and place notes, and ask the class: 'Which part of the matatu puzzle does this belong to: A, B or C?' Highlight a question about radio waves and the Ngong Hills: 'Hold that idea. A reflected wave may matter for the signal.' Do not answer new questions; mark them as 'to be investigated'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with categorisation: learners link new evidence to the big question and see which puzzles are still unresolved. This keeps motivation and gives the lesson sequence a purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check sticky notes: each learner has one 'we learned' and one 'we wonder'. Indicator: at least 70% of new questions are testable and link to A, B or C; look for questions that distinguish reflection from bending (diffraction) or about the radio signal.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model in groups, adding to Part A (corner/diffraction) an arrow diagram showing reflected sound: a ray from the matatu hitting a building wall and bouncing towards the street, with i = r. They label 'reflection helps some sound reach us' and add a note: 'Reflection alone cannot explain why sound spreads into the 4.0 m opening behind the wall; we need another idea.' In Part C they add a possible clue: 'radio waves may also reflect, e.g. off the Ngong Hills'. Part B (pitch) gets a question mark: 'Reflection does not change the pitch of the horn'. Groups complete a 'What we know now / What we still need to explain' box and gallery-walk.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use arrows and labels. Show where reflection fits into the matatu story.' Provide large paper and markers. WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups start so they plan. Circulate and ask: 'Where does the sound go after it hits the wall? What angle?' Cold-call 3 groups to explain their revised Part A. During the gallery walk ask each learner to give one piece of feedback. Close: 'Reflection can send sound back to us, but we still cannot say why we hear the matatu when we are not in line of sight, why the pitch changes, or why the signal fades. Next, refraction.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative model revision and gallery walk: learners externalise their thinking as diagrams, mark the limits of the model and receive peer feedback. Showing the gaps keeps the evidence sequence going into Lesson 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: a ray diagram with i = r, a statement that echo/reflection is part of the explanation, and explicit gaps for B and C. Indicator: all groups add at least one correct reflection element to Part A and one open question. Exit ticket: 'A sonar pulse returns in 0.020 s in water (1500 m/s). How deep?' (15 m).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: Did learners remember to halve the total distance, or did they use d = vt? Which group explained 'there and back' best, and can they help others next time? Did the 17 m minimum make sense after the 10 m test? Did any learners think reflection explains the whole corner puzzle, and how did the DQB help them see its limits? Were the Kenyan contexts (Lake Victoria sonar, halls) engaging? Note which DQB questions to use in Lessons 5 to 8, especially those about bending of waves, and adapt your stopwatch use if timing was inaccurate.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a clap 85 m from a wall returns as an echo after 0.50 s, that a closer wall gives a delay too short to hear separately, and that a Lake Victoria sonar pulse returned after 0.040 s.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that sound reflects from hard surfaces following the law of reflection, that d = vt/2 because the sound travels there and back, that a separate echo needs at least 17 m in air, and that hard and soft surfaces change how a hall sounds.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the sonar depth is 1500 x 0.040 / 2 = 30 m and that reflection can send some matatu sound along the street, but reflection alone does not explain why sound reaches people around the 4.0 m opening, why the horn pitch changes, or why the FM signal fades.

LESSONS.title: Refraction: Speed and Direction Change
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (double period 80 minutes recommended if the ripple tank is set up live)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: refraction, boundary, wave speed, normal, angle of incidence, angle of refraction, ripple tank, deep water, shallow water, wavefront, bending toward the normal

slo.purpose: Learners investigate what happens when waves cross a boundary between two media or depths. They find that a change in wave speed at the boundary causes a change in direction (refraction), and that a wave slowing down bends toward the normal. This gives them the idea of waves changing behaviour at boundaries, which supports the later puzzles about the matatu corner, the pitch and the fading radio.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (a) state that refraction is a change of direction of a wave caused by a change of wave speed at a boundary; (b) state that a wave bends toward the normal when it slows down and away from the normal when it speeds up; (c) use ripple tank data (deep water v = 0.30 m/s, shallow water v = 0.20 m/s, frequency 10 Hz in both) to explain why the wavefronts bunch closer together and change direction in shallow water; (d) describe qualitatively that a light ray in air striking water at 40 degrees bends toward the normal to about 29 degrees.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (drawing wavefront and ray diagrams with the normal); planning and carrying out investigations (observing the ripple tank and the PhET Bending Light simulation); analysing and interpreting data (comparing speeds and angles); constructing explanations; communication and collaboration in groups of four.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how waves behave at boundaries; open-mindedness when revising predictions after evidence; respect for the ideas of peers (value: Respect); responsibility when sharing roles in group work (value: Responsibility); careful and honest observation and recording of data.
slo.keyInquiry: How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 2 and 3 gave learners rays, wavefronts, the normal and angles, and the law of reflection. Lesson 5 adds a second thing waves do at a boundary: they can enter the new medium and change speed and direction. This extends the class model (Part A, how waves behave at boundaries, and the idea that wave speed matters). Learners meet the idea that wave behaviour depends on wave speed and wavelength, which prepares for Lesson 6 (calculations with v = fλ and n = sin i / sin r) and later lessons on diffraction, interference and the Doppler effect. Refraction is a different idea from diffraction, and the lesson makes sure the two are not confused: the matatu music turning the corner is NOT explained by refraction.
slo.safetyNotes: Ripple tank: keep the mains lamp and power supply away from water spills; use a dry cloth for the floor; do not touch the lamp or sockets with wet hands. Use shallow trays on stable benches. Glass or perspex blocks should be handled by the edges. Do not look directly into the lamp or torch beam. Charge laptops or phones before the lesson for the offline PhET simulation. Report broken glass or spills to the teacher immediately.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau begins by reminding the class of the Nairobi street puzzle: Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the building, the horn pitch changes as Baraka drives past at 15 m/s, and the FM radio fades near the Ngong Hills. He explains that today the class studies one more thing waves do: what happens when they cross from one medium or depth into another. Learners first predict what will happen to ripple wavefronts and a torch beam when they cross into shallow water or enter water from air. They then observe a ripple tank with a shallow glass plate (deep v = 0.30 m/s, shallow v = 0.20 m/s, both at 10 Hz), the PhET Bending Light simulation (air to water, 40 degrees becoming about 29 degrees, observed qualitatively), and a short video of a pencil or coin in water. In the Explain phase learners use a claim-evidence-reasoning approach to state that refraction is a change of direction caused by a change of speed and that a slowing wave bends toward the normal. They add new questions to the Driving Question Board, and in the Model Building phase they add a refraction entry to the class model, deciding honestly which part of the Nairobi puzzle it does and does not explain.

framework.learnerExperience: (8 minutes) Learners sit in groups of four. Mr Kamau shows a picture of a ripple tank with deep water on one side and a shallow glass plate on the other, and a torch shining at an angle on a clear tank of water (the torch beam hits the water surface at 40 degrees to the normal). Learners recall the Nairobi scene: Wanjiru and Otieno hearing the matatu music around the corner. Individually, in their notebooks, they draw (1) how they think straight ripple wavefronts moving at an angle will look after crossing into the shallow region and (2) the path of the torch beam after it enters the water. They write one sentence beginning 'I think the wave will ... because ...'. Groups compare drawings and agree on a group prediction, marking the normal as a dashed line and labelling angles.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Yesterday we used rays, wavefronts and the normal. Today the matatu waves, the ripples and the torch beam meet something new: a boundary. Before I show you anything, what do you think happens when a wave crosses into a different medium?' Hand out prediction sheets. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before anyone speaks. Say: 'Draw first, talk second.' Circulate and ask: 'Where did you draw the normal? Does your ray bend toward it or away from it? Why?' Cold-call 3 groups to share predictions and record them on the board under 'Our predictions' without saying who is correct. Say: 'Keep your drawing. We will come back to it with evidence.' Probe with: 'Do you think the wave changes speed? What would that do?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual then group drawing. Committing to a prediction in a drawing makes learners' existing ideas visible, so surprises in the evidence stage create genuine conceptual change. Writing a reason ('because ...') trains learners to link ideas to mechanisms rather than guess.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners drawing the normal correctly as a dashed line perpendicular to the boundary (Lesson 3 skill); (2) whether predictions show bending, no bending, or reflection only; (3) whether any learner mentions speed in their reasoning. Tally on a clipboard how many predict 'toward the normal', 'away', 'straight on' and 'no idea'. Note common ideas such as 'light and waves always go straight' or 'the wave gets stopped by the boundary'. Use this tally to decide how much time to spend on the ripple tank.

framework.learnerExperience: (14 minutes) Three short stations or demonstrations, rotated or shown to the whole class. Station 1, Ripple tank: Mr Kamau sets the vibrator at 10 Hz. Learners watch straight waves in deep water (wavelength 3.0 cm, v = 0.30 m/s) approach a submerged glass plate at an angle, making shallow water. They observe wavefronts closer together in the shallow region (wavelength 2.0 cm, v = 0.20 m/s) and the wave direction turning toward the normal. They also see that the vibrator still taps 10 times each second in both regions. Learners sketch the wavefronts before and after the boundary, drawing the normal and measuring a rough angle on each side with a protractor on the screen or paper. Station 2, PhET Bending Light (offline): Learners send a ray from air into water, set the incident angle to 40 degrees, and see the ray bend toward the normal to about 29 degrees (observed qualitatively, with the protractor tool). They try the ray going from water to air and notice bending away from the normal, and try a 0 degree ray to see no bending. Station 3, Video demonstration: a pencil in a glass of water, and a coin that appears when water is poured into a cup. Learners record observations in a table: Situation, speed before and after, bends toward or away from the normal, wavelength before and after. Link: Wanjiru says, 'So waves can change when they cross something.' Learners record one question about how this connects to the matatu puzzle.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are scientists collecting evidence. Watch the wavefronts, not just the ripples.' At the ripple tank ask: 'What do you notice about the spacing of the wavefronts in the shallow region? What is the vibrator frequency in each region?' Wait 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 learners during the ripple observation: 'What happened to the wavelength?' 'What happened to the direction?' Use a stroboscope or freeze-frame (phone video paused) if available. At the PhET station say: 'Set 40 degrees. Read the refracted angle. Is it bigger or smaller than 40?' Ask: 'What happens if the ray hits the water straight on, at 0 degrees?' Check that learners record the speeds (0.30 m/s and 0.20 m/s) as given data, and that they note light slows in water but do not calculate yet (Lesson 6 does the calculations). Say: 'Draw what you SEE, not what you expected.' Move between groups and ask: 'Does your evidence match your prediction? What changed your mind?' Avoid explaining diffraction here: if a learner asks about the corner, say: 'Great question, put it on the Driving Question Board. Today we are looking at crossing into a new medium, not going around a corner.' Keep safety rules on water and electrical equipment visible.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured evidence gathering using multiple representations (live ripple tank, simulation, video). Seeing the same pattern with water waves and light helps learners notice what stays the same across different waves, which is the start of generalising a rule. Recording data in a table forces attention to the variables: speed, wavelength, frequency and angle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners correctly sketch wavefronts closer together in shallow water; (2) learners state that the frequency stays at 10 Hz; (3) learners read about 29 degrees from the simulation for a 40 degree incident ray and describe it as 'bent toward the normal'; (4) learners record bending away from the normal when going from water to air. Check notebooks for the data table and for the normal drawn on each sketch. Ask 3 learners at random: 'Where is the normal on your diagram?' Note any learner who measures angles from the surface instead of from the normal and correct at once.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 minutes) Groups use the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework on a half-sheet. Claim: 'What does a wave do when it crosses a boundary where its speed changes?' Evidence: they cite at least three observations, for example: deep water v = 0.30 m/s, shallow v = 0.20 m/s, wavefronts bunched closer (3.0 cm to 2.0 cm), frequency stayed 10 Hz, ripple direction turned toward the normal, light at 40 degrees in air bent to about 29 degrees in water. Reasoning: they explain why a change of speed leads to a change of direction by using a wavefront picture: the part of the wavefront that reaches the slower region first slows down while the rest is still fast, so the wavefront swings round and the ray turns toward the normal. A marching-line demonstration helps: four learners link arms and walk from a smooth floor (fast) onto a patch of carpet or sand (slow) at an angle; the line swings. Learners then compare with their predictions and write what they have changed. Finally they answer: 'Does refraction explain why Wanjiru and Otieno hear the music around the building? Why or why not?' They decide that the music turning the corner is a different behaviour (the class will study it later) because here the wave goes into a new medium and changes speed, while at the corner it stays in air.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Write a claim you can defend with evidence. Number your evidence.' Model one CER example with a different context: a wave moving from smooth tarmac road to a muddy track at Ngong. Run the marching-line demonstration with four learners and say: 'Which end of the line hits the slow patch first? What happens to that end? Which way does the line turn?' Wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups to read their reasoning aloud and ask the class: 'Do you agree? What evidence supports it?' Write the key statement on the board: 'Refraction is a change of direction caused by a change of wave speed at a boundary. A wave that slows down bends toward the normal.' Ask: 'What would happen if the wave sped up instead?' (bends away). Check for the misconception that the frequency changes: 'The vibrator taps 10 times each second in both regions. So what changed: frequency, wavelength or speed?' Ask: 'Is refraction the reason the music turns the corner? Turn and talk for 1 minute.' Cold-call 2 learners. Say clearly: 'We will solve the corner puzzle in later lessons. Today we have one tool: refraction.' Do not teach the equation n = sin i / sin r or the wave equation calculations in this lesson; those belong to Lesson 6.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) plus an analogy (the marching line). CER makes learners connect each claim to specific data, strengthening scientific argumentation. The marching-line analogy gives a physical mechanism for why a speed change causes a direction change, so the rule 'slows down, bends toward the normal' is understood rather than memorised. Asking whether refraction explains the corner puzzle trains learners to test an idea against the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check CER sheets for: (1) a claim that mentions both speed change and direction change; (2) at least three correct pieces of evidence using the given numbers (0.30 m/s, 0.20 m/s, 10 Hz, 3.0 cm, 2.0 cm, 40 degrees, about 29 degrees); (3) reasoning that links the slower side of the wavefront to turning. Use a 3-point check: 3 = all parts correct, 2 = partly correct, 1 = unclear. Listen for the correct statement that frequency stays the same. Exit ticket on a slip: 'A wave goes from deep to shallow water. Does it bend toward or away from the normal? Why?' Aim for at least 80% correct; reteach with the marching line if below that.

framework.learnerExperience: (4 minutes) Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the central question: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' Each group writes one new question on a sticky note that came from today's evidence, for example: 'Does the speed of sound change in air, so does sound refract?' 'If waves slow down in shallow water, why does the music still bend around the building?' 'Is the bending of the horn pitch related to speed change?' 'Can the FM signal be bent by the hillside?' They place the notes under the headings Corner (A), Pitch (B) or Signal fading (C), or in a new column 'Waves at boundaries'. They also star earlier questions that today's evidence has partly answered or ruled out, for example 'Is the music bent by something changing its speed?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. What did we learn today that helps with our big question? What new question do we have?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups write. Cold-call 3 groups to read their sticky notes and ask: 'Which part of the matatu puzzle does your question belong to?' Sort the notes with the class. Point to an earlier question about the corner and ask: 'Does refraction answer this one? What is missing?' Prompt: 'Is there a question that refraction can answer for us, and a question it cannot?' Praise careful questions that refer to evidence. Say: 'Notice we are now sure about one thing: crossing into a new medium changes speed and direction. Which parts of the puzzle are still open?' Make sure the questions about Doppler pitch and interference fading are left for later lessons.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with categorising of questions. Learners generate new questions from evidence and sort them against the phenomenon, so they can see their progress and the gaps in their understanding. This keeps the whole sequence coherent and student-driven.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that sticky notes are testable and linked to today's evidence (for example, mention speed, bending, or medium) and not just 'why does the matatu sound change?' Count how many groups can place their question in the correct category (A, B, C or boundaries). Note whether any learner recognises that refraction alone does not explain the music at the corner. Record names of learners who contribute questions, to support quieter learners next time.

framework.learnerExperience: (4 minutes) Learners add to the class model, which has three parts: A (corner/diffraction), B (pitch/Doppler) and C (signal fading/interference). In their notebooks they draw a small box labelled 'Waves at a boundary: refraction' under the model. They draw a diagram showing deep water to shallow water with a dashed normal, wavefronts and a ray bending toward the normal, with the values 0.30 m/s and 0.20 m/s and the note 'frequency 10 Hz stays the same'. They add a second diagram of a ray from air into water at 40 degrees bending to about 29 degrees. Beneath, they write: 'Refraction is a change of direction caused by a change of wave speed at a boundary. A wave that slows down bends toward the normal.' They then add a status note on each part of the model: Part A, 'Refraction is not the reason the music turns the corner, we still need to find out why'; Part B, 'no change yet'; Part C, 'no change yet'. They add one sentence on how this tool might be useful later.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our class model has three parts. What do we add today, and where does it go?' Wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to describe the new box in their own words. Ask: 'What does the model now say about speed and direction? Which part of the Nairobi puzzle does it help with, and which part does it not help with yet?' Insist on honest labelling: 'Do not stretch refraction to explain the corner. A good model says what it cannot do yet.' Provide a sentence frame: 'When a wave slows down at a boundary, it ...'. Collect two model drawings to display on the wall. Preview: 'Next lesson we calculate with v = fλ and n = sin i / sin r to see exactly how much the wavelength and angle change, including the 40 degrees to 29 degrees for light in water and the 3.0 cm to 2.0 cm in the ripple tank.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with explicit limits. Adding a new element and recording what the element does and does not explain keeps the class model evidence-based, teaches that scientific models grow gradually, and prevents over-generalising a new idea to the whole phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: (1) a labelled diagram with the normal, wavefronts and ray bending toward the normal in the slower region; (2) the correct speeds 0.30 m/s and 0.20 m/s and frequency 10 Hz stated as unchanged; (3) the correct rule statement; (4) an honest note that refraction does not by itself explain the music at the corner, the pitch change or the FM fading. Give each learner a quick rating: complete, partly complete, needs support. Plan a short reteach for learners who draw the ray bending away from the normal in the slower medium.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did learners see that the frequency stayed at 10 Hz while the speed and wavelength changed? If not, replay the ripple tank video and ask them to count taps per second. (2) How many learners predicted correctly, and how many changed their ideas because of the evidence? (3) Did any learners confuse refraction with diffraction or reflection? Note examples to address in Lessons 6 and 7. (4) Did every learner measure angles from the normal rather than from the surface? (5) Were all learners able to take part in the group work and the marching-line demonstration, including quieter learners and learners with limited access to devices? (6) Did the offline PhET simulation run smoothly on the available devices, and is a back-up needed? (7) Did the cold-calls and WAIT TIME give enough thinking time? Plan the next lesson by preparing the numbers for calculation: 10 Hz, 3.0 cm to 2.0 cm, n = 1.33, 40 degrees to 29 degrees, 2.26x10^8 m/s.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the ripple tank, waves moved from deep water (v = 0.30 m/s, wavelength 3.0 cm) into shallow water (v = 0.20 m/s, wavelength 2.0 cm) at 10 Hz, and the wavefronts bunched closer and the direction turned toward the normal. In the PhET simulation a light ray in air at 40 degrees entered water and bent to about 29 degrees, toward the normal; going from water to air it bent away.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Refraction is a change of direction of a wave caused by a change of wave speed at a boundary. A wave that slows down bends toward the normal; a wave that speeds up bends away from the normal. The frequency stays the same while the speed and wavelength change.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Refraction describes how waves behave when they enter a new medium or depth, but it does not explain why the matatu music is heard around the building, because the sound stays in the same air. We still need other ideas to explain the corner, the pitch change and the fading radio signal near the Ngong Hills.

LESSONS.title: Refraction Calculations and the Bent Straw: Why Wavelength Changes but Frequency Does Not
LESSONS.aresKeywords: refraction, refractive index, wave equation v = fλ, frequency constant, wavelength change, bent straw, Snell's law, speed of light in water

slo.purpose: To use the wave equation v = fλ and the relation n = sin i / sin r to show that when a wave is refracted its frequency stays the same while its speed and wavelength change, and to use this to explain the bent straw. This strengthens the wavelength and v = fλ reasoning that Lessons 7 to 9 will need for the matatu puzzles.
slo.knowledge: Learners will: (1) state that frequency does not change when a wave crosses a boundary, because the source sets the frequency; (2) use v = fλ to calculate the wavelength in shallow water (10 Hz, 0.20 m/s gives 2.0 cm, compared with 3.0 cm in deep water at 0.30 m/s); (3) use n = sin i / sin r to calculate the refracted angle for light entering water (n = 1.33, i = 40 degrees gives r of about 29 degrees); (4) calculate the speed of light in water, 3.0x10^8 / 1.33 = 2.26x10^8 m/s; (5) explain the bent straw as refraction of light leaving water.
slo.skills: NGSS Science and Engineering Practices: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking (applying v = fλ and n = sin i / sin r), Analyzing and Interpreting Data (comparing ripple tank measurements), Constructing Explanations (the bent straw), Developing and Using Models (revising Model Part A). Practical skills: measuring angles from the normal, reading a ripple tank, using a calculator for sine values.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday optical illusions, precision and honesty with numbers and units, perseverance in multi-step calculations, willingness to revise a prediction when evidence contradicts it, respect for peers' ideas during discussion.
slo.keyInquiry: How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 5 showed that refraction is a change of direction caused by a change of wave speed at a boundary. Lesson 6 makes that idea quantitative: speed and wavelength change while frequency stays constant, which strengthens the v = fλ tool. Lessons 7 and 8 use wavelength to explain why sound diffracts around the 4.0 m opening while light does not; Lesson 9 uses it for FM fading. For the driving question, learners now know that a wave's frequency is set by its source and that wavelength depends on speed. This prepares them to think about the matatu horn, which is at 400 Hz, and its wavelength of 0.85 m.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep the ripple tank away from electrical sockets and wipe up spills straight away to avoid slipping. Use low-voltage lamps and vibrators only. Glass blocks and beakers should be handled with care and carried with two hands. Never look directly at the Sun or a bright torch beam. Use plastic straws and clear plastic cups rather than glass where possible.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau opens by reminding the class of the street scene: Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the corner, the pitch seems to change, and the FM station fades. He tells them they now need a reliable tool for linking speed, frequency and wavelength. In Lesson 5 they saw that waves bend when their speed changes. Today they ask: by how much, and what stays the same? Learners first predict what happens to frequency, speed and wavelength when ripples go from deep to shallow water and what a straw in water will look like. They then observe the ripple tank (10 Hz in both depths), measure the wavelengths of 3.0 cm and 2.0 cm, and carry out a ray-box and glass-block activity for light going from air into water. In the Explain phase they calculate wavelength with v = fλ, the refracted angle with n = sin i / sin r, and the speed of light in water of 2.26x10^8 m/s, and then explain the bent straw in a cup of water. They add questions to the Driving Question Board and revise Model Part A (corner/diffraction) by adding a note that wavelength depends on speed and frequency is fixed by the source. The lesson does not yet explain diffraction at the corner (Lessons 7 and 8), interference (Lesson 9) or the Doppler effect (Lesson 11).

framework.learnerExperience: (About 12 minutes) Learners sit in groups of four. Mr Kamau shows a plastic straw standing in a clear cup of water, viewed from the side, and recalls the matatu scene on a busy Nairobi street. Each learner privately writes predictions on a Predict Sheet: (1) When ripples made by a 10 Hz vibrator move from deep water into shallow water, where they travel more slowly (0.30 m/s in deep water, 0.20 m/s in shallow water), what happens to the frequency? The wavelength? (2) Why does a straw in water look broken at the surface? (3) Is the straw really bent? They draw a quick sketch to show what they think a ray of light does as it passes from air into water. Groups then compare predictions and agree on one group claim on a mini-whiteboard. Learners link this to the matatu puzzle by writing one sentence: 'If waves change speed, what might change about them that could matter for a sound turning a corner?'
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the straw and say: 'Look carefully. Is this straw really broken? Write your own idea first. Do not talk yet.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, silently counting, before taking any answers. Then say: 'Last lesson we saw that waves bend when their speed changes. Today we ask by how much, and what stays the same.' Circulate and record misconceptions you hear, such as 'the frequency gets smaller in shallow water' or 'the straw really bends in water'. Cold-call 4 groups to read their claims without evaluating them: 'Group 2, what did you decide about the frequency, and what makes you say so?' Write the claims on the board under 'Our predictions'. Say: 'Keep these. We will test them with evidence today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a private write-first routine. Committing to a prediction in writing before the evidence creates cognitive conflict if the prediction is wrong. It makes learners' existing ideas visible so they can later be compared with data. Group claims on whiteboards encourage learners to argue from reasoning, not from authority.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) the number of learners who write that frequency stays the same, decreases, or increases, and tally the responses on the board; (b) whether sketches show light bending at the water surface or the straw physically bending; (c) whether learners use words from Lesson 5 such as speed, normal or bending; (d) whether the whiteboard claims include a reason. Indicator of readiness: at least half of the groups give a reason that mentions speed. Note common misconceptions for follow-up in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 25 minutes) Learners rotate through two stations in their groups, about 10 minutes each, then share data. Station A: Ripple tank. Using the vibrator at 10 Hz, learners watch the plane waves cross from deep water into a shallow region (a glass plate under the water). They use a stroboscope or photo of the pattern with a ruler to measure the wavelength in deep water (3.0 cm) and in shallow water (2.0 cm), count the number of waves passing a point in 10 s to check the frequency (about 100 waves in 10 s, 10 Hz in both), and note that the waves bend toward the normal in the shallow region. They record: frequency 10 Hz in both depths, wavelength 3.0 cm and 2.0 cm, speed 0.30 m/s and 0.20 m/s from the teacher's timing. Station B: Light in water. Learners use a ray box, a semicircular transparent tank or glass block, and a protractor to send a ray into the water at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees, measuring the refracted angle of about 29 degrees from the normal. They record i and r in a table for 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees and calculate sin i and sin r. They then view the straw in the cup from different sides and sketch what they see. Data are entered on a class chart.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the rotation say: 'At each station your job is to collect numbers. Measure angles from the normal, not from the surface.' Circulate and ask each group at Station A: 'What is the frequency in deep water? In shallow water? How do you know?' and at Station B: 'What do you notice about sin i divided by sin r as the angle changes?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Ask 3 groups to share their wavelength data and 3 to share their angle data, cold-calling by group number. Prompt: 'Which quantity stayed the same across the boundary? Which two changed?' Say: 'I want you to notice a pattern, not yet explain it.' Ensure safety by keeping water away from sockets and reminding learners to wipe spills. Collect all numbers on a class data chart under headings: Quantity / Deep water / Shallow water.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Collection and Pattern Noticing with a class data chart. Producing the same table of results as a class lets learners see consistent patterns (frequency unchanged, wavelength and speed reduced, sin i / sin r constant) and builds confidence that the pattern is real and not an error by one group. Delaying explanation until after the data are shared keeps the focus on evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) learners measuring angles from the normal correctly; (b) groups reporting frequency of 10 Hz in both depths, wavelengths of 3.0 cm and 2.0 cm, and r of about 29 degrees for i of 40 degrees; (c) learners spotting that sin i / sin r stays about 1.33 for different angles; (d) accuracy of table entries. Indicator: each group can say, without prompting, which quantity did not change at the boundary. Use a checklist while circulating, and note groups needing help with the protractor or with counting waves.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 25 minutes) Using the class data, learners build the explanation step by step. Step 1: Frequency. Learners discuss why the frequency stays 10 Hz: the vibrator sets how many waves are made each second, and the same number of waves per second must cross the boundary, otherwise waves would pile up or vanish at the boundary. Step 2: Wavelength. Using the wave equation v = fλ, they calculate: deep water λ = v/f = 0.30/10 = 0.030 m = 3.0 cm; shallow water λ = 0.20/10 = 0.020 m = 2.0 cm, matching what they measured. Step 3: Refractive index. They use n = sin i / sin r to find the refracted angle: sin 40 degrees = 0.643; sin r = 0.643/1.33 = 0.483; r = about 29 degrees, matching Station B. Step 4: Speed of light in water: n = c/v, so v = 3.0x10^8 / 1.33 = 2.26x10^8 m/s, slower than in air. Step 5: The bent straw. Light from the part of the straw under water bends away from the normal as it leaves the water into air, so the eye traces the rays back in straight lines and sees the straw's underwater part at a shallower apparent position, so the straw looks broken or bent. The straw itself is not bent. Learners write a four-sentence explanation with a labelled ray diagram showing the normal, the bent ray and the apparent position. They then complete a short practice problem set: a Kisumu fisher on Lake Victoria looks at a fish and misjudges its position because of refraction, and a wave with f = 5 Hz and v = 0.25 m/s that slows to 0.15 m/s has wavelength 5.0 cm and then 3.0 cm.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We have numbers. Now let us make sense of them. First, what stayed the same and why?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners: 'Tell me in your own words why the frequency cannot change at the boundary.' If answers are vague, ask: 'If 10 waves leave the vibrator each second, how many must cross the boundary each second?' Model the first calculation on the board with units, then let learners do the second themselves in pairs while you circulate. Ask: 'Using v = fλ, if f is fixed and v falls, what must happen to λ?' Cold-call 2 pairs to show working. For the bent straw say: 'Draw the ray from the straw tip to your eye. Which way does it bend leaving the water and why?' Have 2 learners come to the board to draw the diagram and invite the class to critique it. Address the misconception that the straw really bends by asking: 'How could we check that the straw is straight?' (lift it out). Remind the class that diffraction at the corner is for later lessons; today is only refraction.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) combined with worked-example modelling. Learners state a claim (frequency is constant, wavelength changes), cite evidence from the class data chart, and give reasoning with v = fλ and n = sin i / sin r. Linking calculation to measured values shows that mathematics describes real behaviour and strengthens the connection between the equation and what they observed. Drawing the ray diagram makes the invisible path of light visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) correct use of v = fλ with units: 3.0 cm and 2.0 cm; (b) correct calculation of r of about 29 degrees and v of 2.26x10^8 m/s; (c) a written explanation of the bent straw that states light bends as it leaves water, the eye traces rays straight back, and the straw itself is straight; (d) a diagram with the normal and angles measured from it. Indicator of mastery: learners can answer 'Why does wavelength change but frequency not?' using the source and speed. Use a 3-question exit check (frequency, wavelength, straw) and sort responses into secure, partly secure and not yet secure to plan the next lesson's starter.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 8 minutes) Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board, headed 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' In groups they write on sticky notes: (1) a question that has now been answered by today's evidence (for example 'Does the frequency of a wave change when it enters a new medium?'), and (2) a new question prompted by today's work (for example 'If wavelength changes with speed, what does wavelength have to do with sound bending around the 4.0 m opening?' or 'Why does the matatu horn's frequency seem to change when its source frequency is steady?'). They place the notes on the DQB under the three headings Corner (A), Pitch (B) and Signal fading (C), and move answered questions to an 'Evidence so far' area with a note of the lesson number.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Which of our questions did today's evidence help to answer? Which new questions have appeared?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups write. Cold-call 4 groups to read one note aloud and explain where to place it. Ask: 'Does this note belong with Corner, Pitch, or Signal fading?' Point out that the wavelength question links to Part A, to be investigated in Lessons 7 and 8. Praise precise questions and help refine vague ones: 'Can you make that question testable?' Do not answer the new questions yet; say, 'We will come back to these in the coming lessons.' Photograph the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with student-generated questions. The board keeps learning visible and purposeful by showing how each lesson's evidence moves the class closer to the driving question. Sorting questions into the three puzzles builds a coherent storyline and gives learners ownership of what to investigate next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) questions that are specific and connected to evidence from today; (b) correct sorting of notes into Corner, Pitch or Signal fading; (c) at least one new question per group linking wavelength to the phenomenon; (d) learners moving answered questions to the 'Evidence so far' area with a lesson reference. Indicator: at least three groups produce a question that links wavelength to bending around the corner, showing they are connecting refraction to the next steps.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 10 minutes) Learners return to the class model, which has three parts: A (corner/diffraction), B (pitch/Doppler) and C (signal fading/interference). In groups they add today's evidence to the model poster. Under a new 'Tools we have' box they write: 'The wave equation v = fλ: the source fixes f; when v changes, λ changes.' and 'n = sin i / sin r; n = c/v.' They add a data note: 10 Hz, 3.0 cm to 2.0 cm, n = 1.33, 40 degrees to 29 degrees, 2.26x10^8 m/s. For Part A they add: 'Wavelength depends on speed and frequency: for the matatu horn at 400 Hz in air, λ = 340/400 = 0.85 m.' They mark with a question mark what is still unknown: why wavelength compared with the 4.0 m opening decides whether waves bend around a corner. Parts B and C are left unchanged except for a note that the tool v = fλ will be needed. Each group draws a small labelled diagram of the bent straw on the model as an example of refraction. Finally, each learner completes the summary table prompt in their notebook.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must always match our evidence. What can we now add and what must we still leave as a question?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to state one addition and its supporting evidence. Challenge: 'Does refraction explain why sound turns the corner? How do you know?' Guide learners to see that it does not yet, because the corner involves a gap and an obstacle, not a change of medium. Keep Parts B and C honest: no Doppler or interference explanation is added yet. Ask learners to use words from Lessons 5 and 6 only. Collect the summary tables as an exit ticket and sample three for feedback before the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Consensus Model Building and revision. Learners add only claims supported by evidence and mark open questions, so the model grows cumulatively and honestly. Linking a mathematical tool to the phenomenon (λ = 340/400 = 0.85 m) shows how new knowledge becomes part of a larger explanation. Marking what remains unknown sets up purposeful investigations in Lesson 7.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) model additions that cite specific evidence (10 Hz, 3.0 cm to 2.0 cm, n = 1.33); (b) correct statement that frequency is constant and wavelength changes with speed; (c) honest question marks for the unexplained parts; (d) the bent straw diagram correctly labelled. Indicator: groups do not wrongly claim that refraction explains the corner effect. Use the summary table exit tickets to identify learners needing a quick revision of v = fλ at the start of Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on these questions: (1) Did learners explain the constant frequency using the idea of the source setting it, or only repeat the rule? Which questions got the best responses? (2) Which learners could use v = fλ and n = sin i / sin r correctly and which struggled with sine values or units (cm and m)? (3) Did any learners still think the straw physically bends, and what evidence changed their minds? (4) Was the ripple tank data clear enough, or do the wave counts need a stroboscope or slow-motion video next time? (5) Were all learners able to take part in the cold-calls and DQB tasks? (6) How well do the learners' new questions prepare them to link wavelength with the 4.0 m opening in Lessons 7 and 8? Plan a brief starter for Lesson 7 that revisits wavelength and the wave equation for learners who were not yet secure.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the ripple tank at 10 Hz, the waves had a wavelength of 3.0 cm in deep water and 2.0 cm in shallow water and bent at the boundary. A ray of light entering water at 40 degrees bent to about 29 degrees from the normal. A straw in water looked broken at the surface.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: When a wave is refracted, its frequency stays the same because the source sets it, while its speed and wavelength change (v = fλ). The refractive index n = sin i / sin r = c/v; for water n = 1.33 and light travels at 2.26x10^8 m/s. Wavelength depends on the speed of the wave and the frequency of the source.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The straw looks bent because light from its underwater part bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, and our eyes trace the rays back in straight lines to a shallower apparent position. The straw itself is straight. This does not yet explain why sound turns the corner, but we now have the tool v = fλ to work out wavelengths, such as 0.85 m for the matatu horn at 400 Hz, which we will use in Lessons 7 and 8.

LESSONS.title: Diffraction: Gap Size and Wavelength
LESSONS.aresKeywords: diffraction, gap width, wavelength, ripple tank, wavefront, v = fλ, spreading, 4.0 m opening, PhET Wave Interference

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how waves spread through gaps and around edges, and discover that diffraction is strongest when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the gap. They meet the 4.0 m street opening as the real gap in the matatu phenomenon, ready to be tested with sound and light in Lesson 8.
slo.knowledge: Diffraction is the spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap. It is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. Frequency and wavelength are linked by the wave equation v = fλ (Lesson 6). In the ripple tank at 10 Hz, deep water has v = 0.30 m/s and λ = 3.0 cm. When the gap is much wider than λ, waves mostly keep travelling straight (Lesson 2), with only slight bending at the edges.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (ripple tank and PhET Wave Interference); measuring and recording gap widths and wavelengths; analysing data to find a pattern (ratio of λ to gap width); using models to predict; constructing an explanation from evidence; communicating findings in diagrams using wavefronts and rays.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about why waves behave differently in different situations; patience and precision in observing; respect for peers' ideas during discussion; teamwork and responsibility when sharing equipment; willingness to revise predictions based on evidence.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 left learners asking why the torch beam is blocked by the wall while the music is still heard around the corner. Lesson 7 gives the first piece of evidence: waves spread through gaps, and the amount of spreading depends on the ratio of wavelength to gap width. The street opening is 4.0 m wide and is introduced here as the real gap. In Lesson 8 learners will compare sound and light wavelengths with this opening to fully explain the corner puzzle. This lesson supplies Model Part A (corner/diffraction) with its rule.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep water away from electrical sockets and the vibrator motor; place the ripple tank on a stable table and wipe up spills at once to prevent slipping. Mr Kamau switches the power on and off. Learners must not look directly into the lamp. Barriers should be handled carefully. Take care with any sound demonstration so that loudness stays at a comfortable level.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau opens with Wanjiru and Otieno's puzzle: they stand around the corner of a building on a busy Nairobi street and hear the matatu music, yet cannot see the matatu, and a torch beam would be blocked. Learners first predict what happens to ripples at 10 Hz (λ = 3.0 cm) when they pass through a wide gap and a narrow gap. They then observe the ripple tank with barriers set at different gap widths, and test the same ideas with PhET Wave Interference, recording the ratio of wavelength to gap width. In the Explain phase they build the rule that diffraction is strongest when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the gap, and are introduced to the 4.0 m street opening as the real gap for the matatu. They add new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise Model Part A, noting that they still need the wavelengths of sound and light to complete the explanation in Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the Lesson 1 puzzle: Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the corner but cannot see the vehicle, and the torch beam would be blocked by the concrete wall. Mr Kamau shows the ripple tank with straight waves (10 Hz, λ = 3.0 cm in deep water) heading towards a barrier with a gap. In pairs, learners draw on a worksheet what they think the wavefronts will look like after passing through (a) a wide gap of 12 cm and (b) a narrow gap of 3 cm. They also write one sentence on which gap will make the waves spread more and why, linking it to the corner behind the building.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Remember Wanjiru and Otieno standing around the corner of the building. Sound reaches them but the torch beam does not. Today we test what waves do when they meet a gap." Display the barrier set-up but do NOT run the waves yet. Say: "Draw what you think the waves look like on the other side. Use wavefront lines, not arrows." Give 3 minutes of silent drawing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: "Which gap do you think spreads the waves more, and why?" Cold-call 4 pairs (two for each prediction) and record predictions on the board without judging them. Ask: "Who has a different drawing from your neighbour? What is different?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-and-Commit with Drawn Models: learners commit a diagram to paper before seeing evidence. This surfaces the common misconception that waves always travel in perfectly straight lines (an over-generalisation from Lesson 2) and creates a cognitive 'need to know' that the later observation resolves.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check worksheets for: (1) wavefronts drawn as lines joined across the gap rather than rays only; (2) whether learners show any spreading beyond the gap edges; (3) whether they link gap size to amount of spreading. Tally on the board how many pairs predict 'narrow spreads more', 'wide spreads more', or 'no spreading at all'. Indicator of readiness: at least half the class can justify their prediction with a reason, even if the prediction is wrong.

framework.learnerExperience: Station 1 (ripple tank): in groups of four, learners use the 10 Hz vibrator, where deep water gives v = 0.30 m/s and λ = 3.0 cm. Using two barriers they set gap widths of 12 cm, 6 cm, 3 cm and 1.5 cm in turn, and sketch the wavefronts after the gap. They measure the gap width, note λ = 3.0 cm, and calculate the ratio λ ÷ gap for each, filling in a table, with a column describing the amount of spreading (very little, some, a lot, almost circular). They also place a single barrier edge in the water and observe whether the waves bend into the 'shadow' behind it. Station 2 (PhET Wave Interference): learners set the slit width and the wavelength and watch waves pass through; they change wavelength while keeping the gap fixed, then change the gap while keeping wavelength fixed. Finally, the class is shown a scale diagram of the street: a concrete wall with a 4.0 m opening, with Wanjiru and Otieno standing around the corner. Learners note that this is the 'real gap' that sound or light must go through or around.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the set-up in 2 minutes, then say: "Change only ONE thing at a time. What stays the same? What changes?" Circulate and ask each group: "What is the wavelength here? What is the gap? Which is bigger?" and "Where on the screen do the waves reach beyond the edges of the gap?" Prompt struggling groups: "Look at the edge of the barrier. Do you see waves entering the shadow?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before offering hints. Pause the class twice to cold-call 3 groups each to report one observation. For PhET, ask: "If you double the wavelength but keep the same gap, what happens to the bending?" Then reveal the street diagram: "This opening is 4.0 m wide. Hold that number in your head; we will use it next lesson." Reinforce safety: only Mr Kamau switches the power.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Table and Controlled-Variable Comparison: learners vary one factor at a time and record the ratio λ ÷ gap, which turns observations into a quantitative pattern. Using two different tools (ripple tank and simulation) lets learners check that the pattern holds across systems, which strengthens the claim.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (1) change only one variable at a time; (2) measure gap widths with a ruler and record units correctly (cm); (3) calculate ratios correctly (for example, 3.0 ÷ 12 = 0.25, 3.0 ÷ 6 = 0.5, 3.0 ÷ 3 = 1, 3.0 ÷ 1.5 = 2); (4) describe the 1.5 cm and 3 cm gaps as giving noticeably circular spreading, the 12 cm gap as mostly straight with slightly curved edges. Checklist entries: accurate table, labelled sketches, and a written statement of the pattern.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their predictions and compare them with the ripple tank results. In groups they complete a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement: Claim: how does gap width affect the spreading of waves of fixed wavelength? Evidence: data from the ratio table (for example, λ = 3.0 cm and a gap of 12 cm gave very little spreading, while a gap of 3 cm gave strong, almost circular spreading). Reasoning: using the idea that each point in the gap acts as a source of new waves and that a narrow gap leaves only a small 'source' so the waves spread out, a wide gap behaves like a straight wavefront with only the edges bending. They state the rule in their own words: diffraction is the spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap, and it is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. They use v = fλ (Lesson 6) to confirm that at 10 Hz and v = 0.30 m/s the wavelength is 0.30 ÷ 10 = 0.03 m = 3.0 cm, and explain why changing frequency would change the wavelength and therefore the bending. Finally, they discuss a preliminary link to the corner: the opening is 4.0 m; a wave of wavelength much smaller than 4.0 m would behave like the wide-gap case, while a wave with λ closer to 4.0 m would spread like the narrow-gap case. They do not yet compute for sound or light.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Let's compare your drawing from the start of the lesson with what we saw. Which prediction was closest?" Ask: "What pattern do you see in the ratio column as the spreading increases?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 5 learners from different groups to state the pattern in one sentence. Push for precise vocabulary: "Use the words 'wavelength', 'gap' and 'diffraction' in your answer." Press on reasoning: "Why does the 12 cm gap hardly spread the waves when the 3 cm gap spreads them a lot?" Check the maths: "Using v = fλ, what is the wavelength at 10 Hz and 0.30 m/s?" Address the misconception that waves 'only go straight' by referring to Lesson 2: "In Lesson 2 we saw straight-line travel in open space; today we see what happens at edges and gaps." Close with: "The street opening is 4.0 m. Is that a wide gap or a narrow gap for a 3.0 cm ripple? For sound, we will need numbers next lesson." Do NOT calculate the sound or light ratios yet; keep that for Lesson 8.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Rule Building: learners write the claim from data and justify it with a mechanism. Comparing the prediction with the evidence supports conceptual change, and linking back to v = fλ strengthens the connection between wavelength and frequency from earlier lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for statements such as 'the smaller the gap compared with the wavelength, the more the waves spread'. Look for correct use of the term wavelength rather than wave size or wave height. Success criteria: CER includes a data point as evidence, states the rule accurately (comparable to or larger than the gap), and correctly calculates λ = 3.0 cm from v = fλ. Misconception to flag: learners saying that waves 'squeeze through' a small gap and so spread, or that bigger waves always spread less.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' In groups they write on sticky notes (a) what they now know about the corner puzzle from today's evidence, and (b) new questions that today's evidence raises, for example: 'What are the wavelengths of the matatu music and of light?', 'Does a higher pitch bend less than a lower pitch?', 'Does the 4.0 m opening count as wide or narrow for sound?'. They place their notes under the Part A (corner/diffraction) column and mark any earlier questions that are now partly answered with a tick and a date.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the board. Which of our earlier questions did today's evidence help us answer, even partly?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking groups to move their notes. Cold-call 4 groups to read one new question aloud, and ask the class: "Which of these can we test with numbers? What measurement do we need?" Group similar questions together and label clusters (for example, 'sound vs light', 'pitch and bending'). Point out that the questions about sound and light wavelengths will be answered in Lesson 8, and that questions about pitch change and radio fading belong to later lessons. Keep the board visible and add today's date.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question Clustering on a Driving Question Board: sorting learner questions into categories makes progress visible and shows how today's evidence connects to the storyline. It gives learners ownership of the investigation and signals what evidence must be gathered next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that questions are testable and linked to today's rule (for example, mention wavelength, gap or sound versus light) rather than vague (such as 'why is sound different?'). Count how many groups propose a question that requires a numerical comparison of wavelength with the 4.0 m gap. Indicator of understanding: learners tick off at least one earlier question as partly answered and justify it with evidence from the ripple tank or PhET.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class model with its three parts: A (corner/diffraction), B (pitch/Doppler), and C (signal fading/interference). Today they revise only Part A. In groups they draw the street from above: the building, the 4.0 m opening, the parked matatu and Wanjiru and Otieno around the corner. They add curved wavefronts spreading beyond the edge of the wall to show diffraction, and write a rule box beneath the diagram: 'Diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap; waves with a wavelength much smaller than the gap travel almost straight.' They add a note about what is still missing: 'We need the wavelengths of the matatu music and of light to decide which case applies.' They leave Parts B and C unchanged except for noting questions that remain.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take out your model from Lesson 1 and Lesson 2. What did we say about the torch beam and the music? What can we add now?" Ask groups to include at least one labelled wavefront and the 4.0 m gap on the diagram. Circulate and prompt: "Where would the waves be if there were no diffraction? Where are they now?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups respond. Cold-call 3 groups to present their Part A revisions in 30 seconds each, and invite the class to say one thing they agree with and one thing to improve. Remind learners: "We do not yet know the wavelengths for sound and light compared with 4.0 m. That is our job in Lesson 8." Collect the models for display.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Gaps Identified: learners update a shared model, include the mechanism (wavefront spreading) and explicitly list what remains unexplained. Naming gaps in the model models scientific honesty and sets up the next lesson's investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Success criteria for Part A: (1) diagram shows curved wavefronts spreading beyond the wall edge; (2) the 4.0 m opening is labelled; (3) the rule on wavelength versus gap is stated correctly; (4) at least one unresolved question is listed. Look for learners who avoid claiming that sound definitely bends and light does not without evidence, since the numbers are still to be compared. Quick exit ticket: 'Complete the sentence: Diffraction is greatest when ____.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believe that waves can only travel in straight lines, and what evidence from the ripple tank changed (or did not change) their thinking? Did groups control one variable at a time, and were the ratio calculations accurate? Did learners confuse the size of the gap with the size of the wave or its amplitude? How well did learners avoid jumping to the sound-versus-light conclusion before the numbers were compared? What adjustments to the questioning and wait time would help quieter learners contribute in Lesson 8?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the ripple tank at 10 Hz (λ = 3.0 cm), waves passing through a wide gap of 12 cm mostly travelled straight, while waves passing through a narrow gap of 3 cm or 1.5 cm spread out in almost circular wavefronts. The PhET simulation showed the same pattern when slit width or wavelength was changed. The street opening around the building is 4.0 m wide.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Diffraction is the spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap. It is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap, and is very small when the wavelength is much smaller than the gap. The wavelength can be found from v = fλ, for example 0.30 ÷ 10 = 0.03 m = 3.0 cm.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: This partly explains Part A of the matatu puzzle: waves can bend around the corner if their wavelength is comparable to the 4.0 m opening. We still need to compare the wavelengths of sound and light with 4.0 m in Lesson 8 to explain why the music is heard around the corner but the torch beam is blocked.
