LESSONS.title: Diffraction and the Corner Puzzle: Why Sound Turns the Corner but Light Does Not
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson); can be extended to a double lesson of 80 minutes for the full model revision
LESSONS.aresKeywords: diffraction, wavelength, gap, 4.0 m opening, wavelength-to-gap ratio, pitch, sound, light, matatu, corner, model revision

slo.purpose: To use the diffraction rule from Lesson 7 to compare the wavelengths of sound and light with the 4.0 m street opening, so learners can explain why Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the building while a torch beam from the matatu is blocked by the wall.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (a) calculate the wavelength of sound from the wave equation v = fλ using v = 340 m/s (400 Hz gives 0.85 m, 200 Hz gives 1.7 m, 1000 Hz gives 0.34 m); (b) compare each wavelength with the 4.0 m opening by calculating the ratio λ/gap (0.85/4.0 = 0.21 for the 400 Hz horn); (c) explain that sound with wavelength 0.34 m to 1.7 m is comparable to the opening and diffracts clearly, while visible light of 5.0x10^-7 m (ratio about 1.3x10^-7) hardly diffracts; (d) state that low pitches (long wavelength) bend around the corner more than high pitches (short wavelength).
slo.skills: NGSS Science and Engineering Practices: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking (calculating wavelengths and ratios with v = fλ); Analysing and Interpreting Data (comparing ratios in a table); Constructing Explanations (using the diffraction rule as the reasoning); Developing and Using Models (revising Part A of the class model). Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration; Digital literacy (PhET Sound Simulation).
slo.attitudes: Values: Responsibility (each group member plays an assigned role: calculator, recorder, reporter, checker) and Respect (listening to peers' reasoning and disagreeing with evidence, not opinion). Curiosity about everyday sound and light in Nairobi streets. PCI: Safety and Security Education (stay on the pavement and never stand in the road when observing matatus; keep sound volumes safe for ears).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life? (Focus today: how do sound and light waves behave when they meet the wall and the 4.0 m opening, and why do they behave differently?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 raised the question of why the torch beam is blocked by the wall but the music is heard; Lesson 7 gave the rule that diffraction is greatest when wavelength is comparable to or larger than the gap. Lesson 8 applies that rule with real numbers to the 4.0 m opening and completes the evidence for Part A (corner/diffraction) of the class model. It leaves Part B (pitch change, taught in Lesson 11) and Part C (signal fading, taught in Lesson 9) open and added to the DQB.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Keep speaker or phone volume moderate (never above a comfortable conversation level) during the sound demonstration. Do not look directly into the torch beam, and do not shine it into anyone's eyes. If doing the corner walk outdoors, stay within the school compound, away from the road, and keep learners in sight of the teacher.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau returns to the puzzle that Wanjiru and Otieno met on the Nairobi street: they cannot see the matatu behind the building, yet they hear its music clearly, while a torch beam from the matatu would be blocked by the wall. Learners first predict which wavelengths will bend around the corner and whether high or low pitches will be heard better. In the Observe Phase they gather evidence in three ways: a short corner demonstration with a speaker playing a low tone and a high tone behind a classroom partition (or door) beside a torch; a calculation table where they use the wave equation v = fλ with 340 m/s to find the wavelengths of the horn (400 Hz, 0.85 m) and the music (200 Hz, 1.7 m and 1000 Hz, 0.34 m), then compare each with the 4.0 m opening, giving ratios such as 0.85/4.0 = 0.21; and a comparison with visible light of wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m, whose ratio to the opening is about 1.3x10^-7, essentially no bending. In the Explain Phase learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning explanation of why sound turns the corner and light does not, and explain why high pitches bend less than low pitches. They add a question to the Driving Question Board and revise Part A of the class model. Parts B (pitch/Doppler) and C (signal fading/interference) are only flagged as still open.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the street scene: Wanjiru and Otieno stand around the corner, the matatu is hidden behind the concrete wall, and the 4.0 m street opening is the gap the sound passes through. Individually, in their notebooks, they answer three prediction prompts: (1) Will the 1000 Hz music bend around the corner as well as the 200 Hz music? (2) Which will bend more, the sound or a torch beam? (3) What do you think decides how much a wave bends? They sketch a top-view diagram of the building, the 4.0 m opening, the matatu and the students, drawing arrows for how they think sound and light travel. They then share with a partner and note any disagreements for later testing.
framework.teacherMoves: Display a top-view diagram of the street on the board. Say: "Wanjiru and Otieno can hear the matatu but cannot see it. In Lesson 7 we found a rule about wave size and gap size. Before I give you any numbers, predict: will a high pitch or a low pitch be heard better around the corner? Write your prediction and one reason." Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds after the question before taking any answer. Pair-share for 1 minute. Cold-call 4 learners (2 who predict low pitch, 2 who predict high pitch) and record their predictions in two columns on the board without judging. Say: "Hold on to these predictions, we will test them with evidence today." Circulate and note any learners who say that sound simply 'goes everywhere' so you can probe their reasoning in the Explain Phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain). Writing a prediction and a reason before seeing data surfaces prior ideas, such as 'sound is stronger than light' or 'sound goes everywhere', and makes learners accountable to evidence. Returning to the predictions later lets learners see how their thinking changed, which deepens conceptual change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) learners who connect their prediction to wavelength or the size of the gap, which shows they are using the Lesson 7 rule; (b) learners who give vague reasons like 'sound is louder', which flags a misconception to address later; (c) sketches that show sound arrows curving or spreading past the corner versus a straight torch arrow. Tally predictions on the board (low vs high pitch) to use as a baseline for comparison after the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four with assigned roles (calculator, recorder, reporter, checker) in three stations of about 5 minutes each. Station 1, Corner demonstration: Mr Kamau stands behind a classroom door opened about 1 m (or a partition) with a phone or speaker playing a low tone (about 200 Hz) then a high tone (about 1000 Hz) at equal comfortable volume. Learners sit at an angle in the room where the speaker is not in direct line, and record which tone sounds clearer, and then try the torch from the same position and note that the beam does not reach them. Station 2, Wavelength table: using v = fλ with v = 340 m/s they calculate λ for 200 Hz (1.7 m), 400 Hz horn (0.85 m) and 1000 Hz (0.34 m), then divide each by the 4.0 m opening, getting 0.43, 0.21 and 0.085. Station 3, Light comparison: they take light of wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m, compare it with 4.0 m, compute the ratio of about 1.3x10^-7, and compare it with the sound ratios. They may also use the PhET Sound Simulation to watch waves spread from a source of different frequencies. They complete a class data table of source, frequency, wavelength, ratio to opening, and amount of bending (large, medium, almost none).
framework.teacherMoves: Before the stations say: "Your job is to collect evidence to test your predictions. Every number must go in the table." At Station 1, ask: "Where were you sitting relative to the speaker? Which tone could you hear more clearly? How did the torch behave in the same spot?" At Station 2, model one calculation on the board: "v = fλ so λ = v divided by f; for the horn, 340 divided by 400 equals 0.85 m." Ask: "What do you notice about the wavelength when the frequency goes up?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds before taking answers. At Station 3, ask: "How many times smaller is the light wavelength than the sound wavelength? What does a ratio of about 1.3x10^-7 tell us about bending?" Check units (metres, hertz, m/s) and that learners write 5.0x10^-7 m correctly. Cold-call 3 groups to report their ratio for the 400 Hz horn (0.21) and verify the class agrees. Remind learners: "Stay seated and keep the torch away from faces. Keep the speaker volume low." Where the corner demonstration is hard to hear, move the speaker closer or repeat it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-finding (Analysing and Interpreting Data). Putting frequency, wavelength, ratio and amount of bending side by side lets learners spot that smaller ratios (λ/gap) mean more bending, and that the light ratio is millions of times smaller than the sound ratios. Combining a physical demonstration with calculation links the observation (hearing around the corner) to the quantitative rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners: (a) correctly compute 0.85 m, 1.7 m and 0.34 m using v = fλ with 340 m/s; (b) correctly find the ratio 0.85/4.0 = 0.21; (c) record that the low tone is heard more clearly than the high tone out of line of sight; (d) write the light wavelength as 5.0x10^-7 m and recognise that its ratio is far smaller than for sound. Use a quick checklist for each group. Ask the checker in each group to initial the table to confirm calculations before moving on.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their data table to write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation in their groups: Claim: why Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the building but a torch beam would be blocked. Evidence: the wavelengths 0.34 m to 1.7 m compared with the 4.0 m opening (ratios 0.085 to 0.43, for the horn 0.21), and light at 5.0x10^-7 m (ratio about 1.3x10^-7); and the classroom corner observation. Reasoning: the diffraction rule from Lesson 7, that diffraction is greatest when wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. They then extend the explanation to answer: why do the low pitches of the music bend more than high pitches? (a longer wavelength is closer to the size of the opening). They compare their written claims with another group and revise. Finally, they revisit the Predict Phase tallies and mark which predictions were supported.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use the three-part frame: claim, evidence, reasoning. Your evidence must include at least two numbers from the table." Display sentence starters: "The sound bends because the wavelength of ___ m is ___ compared with the 4.0 m opening..." and "Light does not bend noticeably because...". Circulate and ask: "Why does the ratio matter, rather than the wavelength alone?" and "If the driver played a 1000 Hz tone only, would the students still hear it around the corner? How well?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds after each question. Then run a gallery swap: groups exchange papers and give one 'glow' and one 'grow'. Cold-call 3 groups to read their reasoning aloud and ask the class to give a thumbs up or down if the reasoning uses the Lesson 7 rule. Address the misconception that light does not diffract at all: say, "Light does diffract, but its wavelength of 5.0x10^-7 m is so tiny compared with 4.0 m that the bending is far too small to notice. That is why the torch beam looks blocked." Do not teach the Doppler effect or interference here; if learners ask about pitch change or fading, say, "Great question. Let's put it on the board; we will test it in later lessons."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (Constructing Explanations) with peer critique. Structuring the explanation forces learners to link numerical evidence to a scientific principle rather than just stating a fact. Peer review exposes gaps such as missing numbers or reasoning that mentions only wavelength without the gap size.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 3-point rubric: (1) the claim answers the corner puzzle for sound and light; (2) the evidence cites at least two correct numbers (for example 0.85 m, 4.0 m, 0.21 and 5.0x10^-7 m); (3) the reasoning states that diffraction is greatest when wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. Look for learners who explain why low pitch bends more than high pitch. Note any who confuse wavelength with frequency or say that light 'cannot' bend at all, and follow up with the group.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the question: How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves? In groups they write on sticky notes (a) what they now know about the corner puzzle, and (b) new or remaining questions. They place answered questions in the 'Answered' column with evidence (for example, 'Sound of 0.85 m is comparable to the 4.0 m opening, so it diffracts: ratio 0.21'), and place unanswered questions in 'Still to investigate' (for example, 'Why is the horn higher pitched while approaching?', 'Why does the FM radio fade near the Ngong Hills?'). They may add new questions such as 'Do radio waves of 3.0 m bend around hills?'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the board. Which of our questions have we answered with evidence today? Which ones are still open?" Give each group 3 minutes to write notes. WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds before the first group shares. Cold-call 3 groups to move one sticky note to the 'Answered' column and justify it using a number from today's table. Ask: "What evidence would we need to answer the pitch question?" and "What do the weak radio spots tell us about the signal?" Do not answer these; just record them as questions for the next lessons. Affirm good questions by saying, "That is a testable question."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding. Sorting questions into answered and open shows learners that science progresses through evidence, builds ownership of the storyline, and connects today's finding (Part A) to the next lessons on interference and the Doppler effect.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for sticky notes that cite specific evidence (numbers, ratios) rather than general statements. Check that learners correctly sort the corner question as answered and the pitch and fading questions as open. Note whether new questions are testable and linked to the phenomenon, and whether any learners are still confusing the three puzzles.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise Part A (corner/diffraction) of the one class model. Individually, then in groups, they update their model diagram: a top-view drawing of the building, the 4.0 m opening, the matatu and the two students, showing wavefronts of sound with wavelength 0.85 m spreading and curving around the corner, and a straight arrow for light of wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m blocked by the wall. They add labels for the numbers: λ = 0.85 m for the 400 Hz horn, λ from 0.34 m to 1.7 m for the music, ratio 0.21, light ratio about 1.3x10^-7, and a note that lower pitches bend more than higher pitches. They write a two-sentence caption explaining Part A in their own words. For Parts B and C they leave labelled blank boxes titled 'Pitch change (to be explained)' and 'Signal fading (to be explained)'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Revise only Part A today. Your model must show why sound bends and light does not, using the numbers." Give 8 minutes of work time. Circulate and ask: "Where in your drawing can I see the wavelength compared with the opening?" and "What would change in your model if the matatu played only a 1000 Hz tone?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds before learners respond. Cold-call 3 groups to share their revised Part A and ask others to identify one improvement from their earlier model. Build the class model on a chart by combining the best features: a labelled drawing and a numerical caption. Remind learners to keep Parts B and C blank for later lessons. Finish with an exit ticket: "In one sentence, explain why light from the matatu is blocked by the wall but its music is heard around the corner, using the wavelength and the 4.0 m opening."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (Developing and Using Models). Updating a visual model with quantitative evidence shows how explanations grow stronger over time. Leaving Parts B and C open shows what the model cannot yet explain, which motivates the next investigations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each model: (a) shows curved sound wavefronts around the corner and a blocked straight light ray; (b) uses correct values 0.85 m, 0.34 m to 1.7 m, 4.0 m, 0.21 and 5.0x10^-7 m; (c) states that low pitch bends more than high pitch; (d) leaves Parts B and C unfinished. Use the exit ticket to sort responses into: complete (uses wavelength and gap size), partial (mentions wavelength only), or needs support (says sound is stronger than light). Plan a short revisit for the third group.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners use the ratio of wavelength to gap (not wavelength alone) in their reasoning? Which learners still believe that light cannot diffract, and what evidence helped or did not help them? Was the corner demonstration audible enough for all learners, and should the tone volume or seating be adjusted? How well did the groups manage the calculations with v = fλ and units? Did any learners start explaining the pitch change or the fading radio signal too early, and how did you redirect them? Which questions on the Driving Question Board show the strongest curiosity that you can use to launch Lesson 9 on interference and the fading radio? Note any learners needing extra support with scientific notation (5.0x10^-7 m) before the next lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a low tone (about 200 Hz) was heard more clearly than a high tone (about 1000 Hz) around the corner of the partition, while the torch beam did not reach us. We calculated that the matatu horn (400 Hz) has wavelength 0.85 m, the music ranges from 1.7 m (200 Hz) to 0.34 m (1000 Hz), and light has wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m, compared with the 4.0 m street opening.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. For the horn, the ratio of wavelength to gap is 0.85/4.0 = 0.21, so the sound clearly bends, while for light the ratio is about 1.3x10^-7, so it hardly bends at all. Lower pitches (longer wavelengths) bend around the corner more than higher pitches.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the building because the sound waves of wavelength 0.34 m to 1.7 m are comparable to the 4.0 m opening and diffract around the corner, while the torch beam, with wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m, hardly diffracts and is blocked by the wall. The pitch change and the fading radio signal are still open questions on our Driving Question Board.

LESSONS.title: Interference and the Fading Radio: Loud Spots, Quiet Spots and Weak FM Signal
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (double lesson of 80 minutes recommended if the speaker walk is done outdoors)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: superposition, interference, constructive interference, destructive interference, path difference, wavelength, loud spot, quiet spot, FM radio, Ngong Hills, ripple tank, speakers

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how two overlapping waves combine, so they can explain the loud and quiet spots between two speakers and the fading FM signal near the Ngong Hills (Part C of the class model).
slo.knowledge: Superposition is the adding together of overlapping waves. Interference is the result. Constructive interference (reinforcement) occurs when path difference = nλ. Destructive interference (cancellation) occurs when path difference = (n+1/2)λ. Two speakers playing 340 Hz have λ = 340/340 = 1.00 m, so a path difference of 1.00 m gives a loud spot and 0.50 m gives a quiet spot. FM at 100 MHz has λ = 3.0x10^8/1.0x10^8 = 3.0 m. Direct and hillside-reflected signals cancel at weak spots half a wavelength apart, 1.5 m.
slo.skills: Predicting, observing and recording patterns in a ripple tank; planning and carrying out a walk across a sound field; calculating λ using the wave equation v = fλ and path difference; using evidence to construct an explanation (NGSS SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday signal problems, collaboration in teams, respect for different ideas when predictions are tested, and persistence when results differ from expectations.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 7 and 8 explained why the music turns the corner (diffraction). Lesson 9 answers the third puzzle: why the FM signal fades at certain spots near the Ngong Hills even though the station never changes. It supplies the evidence for Part C of the class model and prepares Lesson 10 (standing waves), which links the 1.5 m spacing to half a wavelength.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep speaker volume moderate, since 340 Hz tones can be tiring and loud tones can harm hearing. Wipe up spilled water around the ripple tank at once to prevent slipping and keep mains-powered equipment dry. Keep learners walking slowly with clear paths when they walk across the room with their eyes on the floor. Switch off the signal generator after use.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau begins by reminding the class of Wanjiru and Otieno's three puzzles. Learners have explained the corner (Lesson 8), so today they tackle the fading FM radio in Baraka's matatu on the Nairobi-Ngong route. Learners first predict what happens when two sets of waves overlap. They then observe two ripple sources in a ripple tank, then walk in front of two speakers both playing 340 Hz and map loud and quiet spots. In the Explain phase they use v = fλ to find λ = 1.00 m, link loud and quiet spots to path differences of 1.00 m and 0.50 m, and then scale the idea to the 100 MHz FM station (λ = 3.0 m) whose direct and hillside-reflected signals cancel at weak spots 1.5 m apart. Learners add questions to the DQB and build Part C of the class model. The lesson does not teach standing waves (Lesson 10) or the Doppler effect (Lesson 11).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the third puzzle: Baraka's FM radio fades and crackles at certain spots near the Ngong Hills and comes in clearly a few metres on, though the station never changes. Individually, learners draw two sets of circular ripples spreading from two dippers and predict in their notebooks what happens where they overlap. Then they predict: 'If two speakers both play the same 340 Hz tone, will the sound be equally loud everywhere in front of them?' They sketch a top-view of the room with predicted loud (L) and quiet (Q) spots. Pairs compare predictions, then share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember Baraka's radio. The station is always 100 MHz. So why would the signal be strong here and weak one step later?' Hold up two stones or draw two dippers on the board. Ask: 'What do you think happens when two waves meet?' Give 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME before anyone speaks, then cold-call 4 learners to share predictions without judging. Record ideas such as 'they add', 'they cancel', 'they bounce off each other' on the board under 'Our predictions'. Ask: 'What would make you change your mind?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain: committing to a written prediction first creates a cognitive conflict that makes learners care about the evidence, and the recorded misconceptions (for example, 'waves bounce off each other') can be revisited and corrected after observation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (1) a drawn overlapping pattern; (2) a stated prediction about loudness (equal everywhere or not); (3) a reason given. Tally on the board how many learners predict equal loudness everywhere versus varying loudness. Note who holds the idea that waves collide and stop.

framework.learnerExperience: Station 1 (ripple tank, 10 minutes): Two dippers on the vibrator produce ripples at 10 Hz. Learners look at the pattern and describe lines of strong disturbance and lines of calm water spreading out from between the sources. They sketch the pattern and mark where crests meet crests and where crests meet troughs. Station 2 (speakers, 12 minutes): Two speakers, side by side, both play 340 Hz from one signal generator. Learners in groups of four take turns: one walks slowly in a straight line about 3 m in front of the speakers with one ear covered, while the others mark with chalk or paper the spots where the sound is loud (L) or quiet (Q). They measure the distance between neighbouring loud spots and between a loud and a quiet spot with a tape measure and record it in a table. They also cover one speaker and note that the quiet spots disappear. Optional: the PhET Sound simulation or LabXchange Wave Interference can be used if equipment is limited.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate and ask: 'Where is the water almost flat? What are the two ripples doing there?' and 'Point to a quiet spot. Is the sound dead, or is a speaker still working?' Prompt: 'Close one ear and walk slowly; mark the spot as soon as the loudness changes.' Ask groups to cover one speaker and listen again, and ask: 'What happened to the quiet spots? What does that tell you?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to report the spacing they measured. Remind learners to keep the volume moderate. Say: 'Remember that the signal generator frequency is 340 Hz. Keep that number, we need it in the Explain phase.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with pattern spotting: learners gather the same observations in two different media (water and sound) so they notice that loud and quiet spots are a property of waves in general, not of one machine.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) sketches that show alternating bands of strong and calm water spreading from between the sources; (2) a table with at least 4 marked spots and measured spacing; (3) learners noticing that covering one speaker removes the quiet spots. Probe learners who say 'the speaker is broken at the quiet spot'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their data in four steps. Step 1: use the wave equation v = fλ with v = 340 m/s and f = 340 Hz to get λ = 340/340 = 1.00 m. Step 2: explain the speakers. For a spot equidistant from both speakers, the path difference is 0, waves arrive crest with crest, and they reinforce (constructive). They are told that at a spot where the path difference is 1.00 m (one whole λ) the waves still arrive in step and the spot is loud, while at a spot where the path difference is 0.50 m (half λ) a crest arrives with a trough, the waves cancel and the spot is quiet (destructive). They write the rules: constructive when path difference = nλ; destructive when path difference = (n+1/2)λ. Step 3: they complete a table for path differences of 0, 0.50 m, 1.00 m, 1.50 m and 2.00 m and label each loud or quiet. Step 4: transfer to the FM radio. They calculate λ for the 100 MHz station: λ = 3.0x10^8/1.0x10^8 = 3.0 m. Near the Ngong Hills, the signal that comes directly to the matatu and the signal reflected from the hillside overlap. As the matatu moves, the extra distance travelled by the reflected signal changes, so the path difference changes between nλ and (n+1/2)λ. The weak spots, where the path difference changes by half a wavelength, are 1.5 m apart. Each learner writes a 3-4 sentence explanation of why Baraka's radio fades and returns while the station never changes, and draws a labelled diagram of the direct and reflected paths.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the wave equation. What are v and f for the speakers?' Cold-call 2 learners for λ and wait 10-15 seconds. Draw two wave paths on the board, one with a 1.00 m difference and one with 0.50 m. Ask: 'If the path differs by exactly one wavelength, do the crests line up or not?' then cold-call 3 pairs. Say: 'Why is the quiet spot not silent everywhere? Think about the two speakers.' Introduce the rules nλ and (n+1/2)λ only after learners have described the pattern in their own words. Challenge: 'Radio waves are not sound. Do you think the same rule applies? What would the wavelength be?' Guide the calculation of λ = 3.0 m and show 1.5 m as half of it. Say clearly that this lesson does not explain why the pattern forms a fixed standing pattern, which is for Lesson 10. Warn against the misconception that 'the signal got weaker because of distance': 'The station power did not change. What changed is how the two signals add up.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with analogy transfer: learners make a claim about the fading radio, support it with speaker evidence and calculations, and reason with path difference. Transferring the same idea from sound (λ = 1.00 m) to radio (λ = 3.0 m) strengthens understanding that interference is a general wave property.
framework.formativeAssessment: Success indicators: (1) λ = 1.00 m calculated correctly with units; (2) learners match path difference 1.00 m to a loud spot and 0.50 m to a quiet spot; (3) the FM wavelength of 3.0 m and the 1.5 m spacing are correct; (4) the explanation mentions two signals (direct and reflected) overlapping and cancelling, not 'the station got weak'. Use a 3-question exit check on mini whiteboards: 'Path difference 1.00 m, loud or quiet?' 'Path difference 0.50 m?' 'What is the spacing of FM weak spots?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board and use sticky notes to (a) place a green dot on questions now answered (for example, 'Why does the radio signal fade at certain spots?'), (b) add new questions that arose (for example, 'Why do the fading spots stay in the same places?', 'Do the weak spots move if the matatu stops?', 'Could we get a quiet spot with a different frequency?', 'Why does the pitch change?'), and (c) group new questions under headings: still about interference, about standing patterns, about pitch change.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which questions can we now answer with evidence from today?' Give 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME, then cold-call 3 learners to move a question and justify it using speaker or ripple data. Invite 3 more to read out new questions. Say: 'Which of these questions will we explore in the next lessons?' Mark the fixed-pattern question as the bridge to Lesson 10 and the pitch question for Lesson 11.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking on the DQB: showing which questions are answered by evidence and which remain makes progress visible and keeps learners connected to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether new questions use today's vocabulary (path difference, cancel, reinforce) and whether learners cite evidence for moving a question. Note any question showing a misconception, for example 'does the radio break at the weak spot?', for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model, adding Part C (signal fading/interference) while Parts A (corner/diffraction) and B (pitch/Doppler) stay on the display. Part C is drawn as a diagram of the matatu on the Nairobi-Ngong road, a direct signal arrow from the transmitter, a reflected signal arrow from the Ngong Hills, and labels: 'λ = 3.0 m', 'constructive: path difference = nλ, strong signal', 'destructive: path difference = (n+1/2)λ, weak signal', 'weak spots 1.5 m apart'. Part B is left with a note: 'Not yet explained'. In groups they add a small inset of the two-speaker loud/quiet pattern as supporting evidence and write one sentence connecting the evidence to the model. They then complete the summary table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model needs a Part C. What must be in it to explain Baraka's radio?' Give 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME, then cold-call 4 learners, each adding one element. Ask: 'What evidence do we have for each label?' Point to the speaker data. Ask: 'Does the model say the radio station changed?' (No.) Check that groups use the 3.0 m and 1.5 m figures exactly. Say: 'Next lesson we will see what happens when waves travel in opposite directions along a guitar string and meet, and why the 1.5 m spacing is half a wavelength.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building: each lesson adds one part of a single class model, so learners see how separate properties of waves (diffraction, interference) combine to explain one real event.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a model checklist: (1) direct and reflected paths drawn; (2) λ = 3.0 m shown; (3) both interference rules stated correctly; (4) 1.5 m spacing labelled; (5) statement that the station does not change. Groups with 4 or 5 ticks are secure; those with fewer need a short conference before Lesson 10.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believed that waves 'bounce off' or 'destroy' each other, and did the covered-speaker test change their minds? Were learners able to calculate λ = 1.00 m and λ = 3.0 m unaided? Did the walk across the sound field give clear loud and quiet spots despite echoes from classroom walls, and how could the setup be improved (for example, moving the activity outside or to the school field)? Which learners confused interference with a weakening of the source, and what additional evidence might help? Did the DQB questions suggest learners are ready for Lesson 10?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the ripple tank, two sources made bands of strong ripples and calm water. With two speakers playing 340 Hz we found loud and quiet spots in the room, and the quiet spots vanished when one speaker was covered.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Overlapping waves add together (superposition). When the path difference is nλ the waves reinforce (constructive interference, loud or strong). When it is (n+1/2)λ they cancel (destructive interference, quiet or weak). For 340 Hz, λ = 1.00 m, so a path difference of 1.00 m gives a loud spot and 0.50 m gives a quiet spot.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Near the Ngong Hills, the 100 MHz FM signal has λ = 3.0 m. The direct signal and the signal reflected from the hillside overlap and cancel at weak spots about 1.5 m apart, then reinforce between them. The radio fades and returns even though the station never changes.

LESSONS.title: Standing Waves and Musical Notes: Guitar Strings, Nodes and the Half-Wavelength Link
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (double lesson of 80 minutes recommended if the model-building phase is extended)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: standing wave, stationary wave, node, antinode, superposition, fundamental, harmonic, string length, tension, pitch, half wavelength, wave equation v = fλ

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how two waves travelling in opposite directions along a string superpose to form a standing wave, and use this to explain how string length and tension set the musical note. They then link the half-wavelength spacing in a standing wave to the 1.5 m spacing of the FM fading spots near the Ngong Hills.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (a) explain that a standing wave forms when a wave and its reflection from a fixed end travel in opposite directions and superpose; (b) identify nodes (no movement) and antinodes (maximum movement) and state that adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart; (c) use L = λ/2 for the fundamental and v = fλ to show that the 0.65 m guitar string with wave speed 143 m/s has fundamental wavelength 1.30 m and frequency 110 Hz; (d) show that the second harmonic has wavelength 0.65 m and frequency 220 Hz (3 nodes, 2 antinodes), and that pressing the string to 0.325 m at the same tension also gives 220 Hz; (e) link the 1.5 m spacing of the weak FM spots to half the 3.0 m wavelength.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (sketching standing wave patterns); planning and carrying out investigations (varying length and tension one at a time); analysing and interpreting data (comparing predicted and measured frequencies); using mathematics (v = fλ, L = λ/2, T = 1/f); constructing explanations; communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how musical instruments such as the nyatiti, guitar and litungu produce notes; responsibility when handling tensioned strings; respect for the ideas of others during group discussion; appreciation of physics in music and communication in Kenya.
slo.keyInquiry: How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 8 and 9 explained the corner puzzle through diffraction and the fading radio through interference. In Lesson 10 learners see what happens when reflected waves keep overlapping with the original wave: a stable pattern of fixed quiet points (nodes) and strong points (antinodes). This deepens Part C of the class model by showing why the quiet spots are half a wavelength apart, and it adds a real application of waves (musical notes) that answers the second KICD key inquiry question. It also prepares learners for Lesson 11 (the Doppler effect) by reinforcing v = fλ.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep the slinky on the floor or a smooth table and never release a stretched end suddenly; it can snap back. Keep faces away from the string when tightening a guitar string and do not over-tighten; wear no loose items near the tuning pegs. Keep slinky stretch to about 3 m and secure one end held by a learner or tied to a table leg. Keep walking space clear of cables if using laptops or tablets for the simulation. Keep the volume low when plucking or using the buzzer.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau reminds the class of Wanjiru and Otieno standing around the corner, hearing the matatu music and then meeting a fading FM radio near the Ngong Hills. In Lesson 9 learners found that weak spots appear where the direct and reflected radio signals cancel. Today the question is: what happens when a wave and its reflection travel along the same line for a long time? Learners first predict what a guitar string of length 0.65 m will do when plucked. They observe standing waves on a slinky and a guitar string, then use the PhET Standing Waves on a String simulation (offline copy) to count nodes and antinodes and vary frequency, tension and length. In the Explain phase they use L = λ/2 and v = fλ to show that the 0.65 m string with wave speed 143 m/s gives 110 Hz, the second harmonic gives 220 Hz, and a string pressed to 0.325 m also gives 220 Hz. They then connect nodes spaced λ/2 apart to the weak FM spots 1.5 m apart (half of 3.0 m). The class updates the Driving Question Board and extends Model Part C with standing-wave ideas.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four. Mr Kamau plucks the guitar string (length 0.65 m) and then presses it halfway along (0.325 m) and plucks again. Learners record individual predictions in their notebooks: (1) Why does the string seem to vibrate in a fixed pattern with some points hardly moving? (2) Will the shorter string give a higher or lower note? (3) If the string is tightened, what happens to the note? Each learner draws a quick sketch of what the string looks like while vibrating. They then link back to the phenomenon by writing one sentence on how this could relate to Wanjiru and Otieno's fading radio spots, where some positions are weak and others are strong.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Last lesson we found that two overlapping waves can make quiet spots and loud spots. Today we ask what happens when a wave bounces back along the same line and keeps overlapping with itself." Pluck the long string, then the pressed string. Say: "Before I tell you anything, write your prediction and draw the string." Give silent WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Then cold-call 4 learners from different groups: "What does your sketch show and why?" Ask 2 learners to state their reasoning for shorter versus longer string. Do not correct predictions; write 3 different ideas on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions'. Say: "Keep these. We will test them with evidence."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-and-sketch with public recording of ideas. Learners commit to a model before instruction, which makes later evidence more meaningful because they can compare it with their own thinking and see changes in their reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether at least 80% of learners wrote a prediction for both length and tension. Look for the misconception that the whole string moves equally or that only the plucked point moves. Note learners who link nodes to quiet spots, or who say a shorter string gives a higher note. Record the number of sketches that show points of no movement.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners rotate through three stations in groups of four, 5 minutes each. Station 1 (slinky): two learners stretch the slinky to about 3 m on the floor and a third shakes one end sideways at a steady rate while the fourth watches. They find the rate that makes the slinky vibrate in one big loop (1 antinode, 2 nodes at the ends), then double the rate for 2 loops (3 nodes, 2 antinodes). They count nodes and antinodes and draw each pattern. Station 2 (guitar string): the 0.65 m string is plucked at full length, lightly touched at the midpoint (0.325 m) and plucked again; learners listen and compare notes. They then tighten the string slightly and note the pitch change. Station 3 (PhET Standing Waves on a String, offline): learners set the fixed-end option, change frequency until the string shows a standing pattern, and count nodes and antinodes. They vary tension and record what happens to the frequency needed. They use data from the established case: L = 0.65 m, v = 143 m/s, to check the simulation setup. Each learner records at least 3 observations in a table: pattern drawn, number of nodes, number of antinodes, and effect on pitch.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "You are not memorising today; you are collecting evidence. Count nodes and antinodes carefully." Circulate and ask: "Where does the slinky not move at all? What do we call those points?" At the guitar station ask: "What changed when you shortened the string? What stayed the same?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before accepting answers. At the simulation say: "Change one thing at a time. What did you change, and what did you observe?" Cold-call 3 learners at stations to describe a pattern they saw. Remind learners about safety: "Hold the slinky end firmly, never release it suddenly." Ensure each group records both slinky patterns and the length-pitch observation. Provide the term 'node' and 'antinode' only after learners describe the points in their own words.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence gathering with a structured observation table (data-first approach). Learners describe patterns in everyday language before receiving vocabulary, building a meaningful link between what they saw and the scientific terms. Multiple representations (slinky, string, simulation) strengthen the pattern across different media.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners can: (a) point to nodes and antinodes on their slinky pattern; (b) count 2 nodes and 1 antinode for the first pattern and 3 nodes and 2 antinodes for the second; (c) state that the shorter string gave a higher note; (d) state that tighter string gave a higher note. Use a tally on the board of groups with correct tables. Listen for learners confusing nodes with antinodes and re-ask guiding questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners consolidate observations into an explanation using a sequence of guided steps. Step 1: In pairs they explain how a standing wave forms: the wave travelling along the string reflects at the fixed end (linking to Lesson 3 reflection) and the reflected wave travels the opposite way; the two waves superpose (linking to Lesson 9 interference), giving fixed nodes where they always cancel and antinodes where they always reinforce. Step 2: Using the guitar string example they calculate. For the fundamental, L = λ/2 so λ = 2 × 0.65 = 1.30 m, and from the wave equation v = fλ, f = 143/1.30 = 110 Hz. For the second harmonic, λ = 0.65 m (3 nodes, 2 antinodes) and f = 143/0.65 = 220 Hz. When the string is pressed to 0.325 m at the same tension, λ = 2 × 0.325 = 0.65 m and f = 220 Hz, a higher note from the shorter string. Step 3: They explain that greater tension raises the wave speed on the string, so for the same length the frequency rises. Step 4 (link to phenomenon): The distance between neighbouring nodes is λ/2. The FM signal has wavelength 3.0 m, so weak spots are half a wavelength apart, which is 1.5 m, exactly the spacing noted near the Ngong Hills. Learners write a four-sentence explanation, then pair-share and revise it.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use your tables as evidence. Where do the two waves meet, and why does the pattern stay in place?" Draw a large diagram of the string with an incident wave and a reflected wave. Ask: "What happens at the fixed end to the reflected wave? Which lesson showed us reflection?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for the formation of the standing wave and 2 learners for each calculation step. Model the first calculation on the board: "L is half a wavelength, so lambda equals 2 times 0.65." Then let learners do the second harmonic and the 0.325 m case independently, checking with a neighbour. Ask: "Why does the 0.325 m string give the same frequency as the second harmonic of the long string?" Then ask: "If nodes are half a wavelength apart and the radio wavelength is 3.0 m, how far apart are the weak spots?" Wait 10-15 seconds and cold-call 2 learners. Do not re-teach interference or reflection; refer back only: "In Lesson 9 we used path difference; in Lesson 3 we saw reflection." Address the misconception that a standing wave does not move energy along the string; say that nodes stay still while antinodes oscillate in place.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with mathematical modelling. Learners state a claim (shorter string, higher note), support it with observation and calculation, and give reasoning using superposition and L = λ/2. This builds a causal chain from reflection to superposition to standing pattern to note, then transfers the half-wavelength idea to the radio fading spots.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect pair-share written explanations. Success indicators: learners correctly state that two waves travelling in opposite directions superpose; they correctly compute 1.30 m and 110 Hz; they compute 220 Hz for both the second harmonic and the 0.325 m string; they state weak FM spots are 1.5 m apart as half of 3.0 m. Watch for errors such as using L = λ instead of L = λ/2, or confusing nodes with antinodes. Do a quick thumbs-up/sideways check on confidence after the calculations.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the question: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' In groups they write on sticky notes (a) new evidence from today, (b) a question that remains. Examples they may post: 'Standing wave nodes are half a wavelength apart, like the weak FM spots 1.5 m apart'; 'A shorter string gives a higher note'; 'Why does the matatu horn sound higher as it comes closer?' They place notes under Part A (corner), Part B (pitch), or Part C (signal fading). Learners also tick off earlier questions that now have answers and mark those that still need evidence, especially the pitch question for Part B.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Go back to our driving question. What can we now explain better than before?" Hand out sticky notes and give 3 minutes. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: "Which part of our puzzle did today's evidence help most?" Cold-call 3 learners to read a note aloud and explain where they placed it. Ask: "Which question is still unanswered?" Highlight that the pitch change (Part B) has no explanation yet and tell learners it is the focus of the next lesson. Sort notes together and star questions that are most frequently asked. Avoid giving the Doppler explanation now; say: "Hold that question for Lesson 11."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of progress. Learners connect new evidence to the anchoring phenomenon and see how knowledge accumulates, which maintains purpose and motivates the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count the number of sticky notes that connect standing waves to Part C (fading signal). Check that at least half the groups post a question about the matatu pitch. Look for notes that correctly state the 1.5 m link or the string-length result. Identify learners whose questions show misconceptions, for example believing standing waves are not caused by reflection.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model, which has three parts: A (corner/diffraction), B (pitch/Doppler), C (signal fading/interference). Today the focus is Part C. In groups they add a diagram showing the direct FM signal (wavelength 3.0 m) and the signal reflected from the Ngong Hills hillside travelling in opposite directions, forming a standing-wave-like pattern with weak spots (nodes) 1.5 m apart and strong spots between them. They label wavelength 3.0 m, spacing λ/2 = 1.5 m, and add a mini panel showing the guitar string analogy: L = λ/2, 110 Hz, 220 Hz, 0.325 m. In Part A and Part B they add a note on what remains unchanged and what is still to be explained (Part B is still incomplete until Lesson 11). Each group adds one 'we still wonder' statement. Groups share their updated Part C diagram in a short gallery walk.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Add today's evidence to Part C. Show how the string helps us understand the radio fading." Remind them: "The reflected signal comes back and overlaps with the direct signal, just like the reflected wave on the string." Give 6 minutes for revision and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking groups to explain their diagram. Cold-call 3 groups to present one change to the model and the evidence behind it. Ask: "What is the same between the guitar string and the FM signal? What is different?" Note that the radio case is similar because of overlapping direct and reflected signals, but do not claim a perfect standing wave in the open air. Prompt learners to leave Part B unfinished and flag what evidence is needed. Close with: "Next lesson we ask why the horn sounded 418 Hz while approaching and 383 Hz while moving away."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative model revision with evidence-based justification. Learners decide what changes in the model and defend each change with data, which strengthens causal reasoning and shows how a single model grows across lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group's Part C diagram includes: wavelength 3.0 m, weak spots 1.5 m apart, link to λ/2, and the idea of direct and reflected signals overlapping. Check that the guitar string values (0.65 m, 143 m/s, 110 Hz, 220 Hz, 0.325 m) are shown correctly. Listen for correct use of the terms node and antinode. Look for at least one group that identifies the limits of the analogy.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners could explain why the pattern stays fixed, in terms of two waves moving in opposite directions, and which still described it as one wave moving? Did learners confuse L = λ/2 with L = λ, and how did the sketches reveal this? How well did learners connect the 1.5 m spacing of weak FM spots to half of the 3.0 m wavelength? Which station (slinky, guitar, simulation) gave the strongest evidence, and what could be improved if equipment was limited? Did learners notice that the shorter string gives a higher note without being prompted? What needs to be revisited before starting the Doppler effect in Lesson 11?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a slinky and a guitar string of length 0.65 m, when shaken or plucked, showed fixed points of no movement (nodes) and points of large movement (antinodes). The fundamental pattern had 2 nodes and 1 antinode; the second pattern had 3 nodes and 2 antinodes. A shorter string (0.325 m) and a tighter string gave a higher note.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a standing wave forms when a wave and its reflection travel in opposite directions and superpose. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, and for the fundamental L = λ/2. With v = 143 m/s on a 0.65 m string, λ = 1.30 m and f = 110 Hz; the second harmonic is 220 Hz, and a 0.325 m string also gives 220 Hz. Length and tension set the note.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explained that the weak FM spots near the Ngong Hills are about 1.5 m apart because the direct and reflected signals overlap, and the 100 MHz signal has wavelength 3.0 m, so weak spots are half a wavelength (1.5 m) apart, just as nodes on a string are λ/2 apart. This strengthens Part C of our model, while the pitch change of the matatu horn (Part B) still needs explaining.

LESSONS.title: The Doppler Effect: Why the Matatu Horn Changes Pitch
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (double lesson: 80 minutes recommended if the moving-buzzer activity is run twice)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: Doppler effect, apparent frequency, relative motion, source speed, wavelength, pitch, compression, rarefaction, ambulance siren, matatu horn, v = fλ

slo.purpose: Learners explain and calculate why the pitch of a moving sound source seems higher on approach and lower on recession, resolving Puzzle 2 of the matatu mystery (the horn heard at 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding although Baraka keeps it at 400 Hz).
slo.knowledge: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the observed frequency of a wave because the source and observer move relative to each other. A moving source compresses wavelengths ahead of it and stretches them behind it. Approaching: f' = f v/(v - vs). Receding: f' = f v/(v + vs). For the matatu (f = 400 Hz, vs = 15 m/s, v = 340 m/s) f' = 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding, a 35 Hz drop. For the ambulance siren (700 Hz at 20 m/s) f' = 744 Hz approaching and 661 Hz receding. The horn itself never changes.
slo.skills: Predicting from prior experience; observing and recording pitch changes; using a model (moving buzzer, wavefront drawings) to explain observations; analysing and interpreting data; using mathematical thinking to apply the Doppler formulas and v = fλ; constructing explanations; communicating using evidence and reasoning.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday sounds on Nairobi roads; respect for peers' ideas during discussion; responsibility and teamwork in the moving-buzzer activity; appreciation of how physics explains daily life (ambulances, matatus, speed checks).
slo.keyInquiry: How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 7 and 8 resolved Puzzle 1 (diffraction at the 4.0 m opening) and Lesson 9 began resolving Puzzle 3 (interference). Lesson 11 resolves Puzzle 2 (pitch change) by building on Lesson 6 (v = fλ, wavelength and frequency) and Lesson 1 pitch observations (418 Hz and 383 Hz heard, values only observed then). Learners now calculate those values and complete Part B of the class model, ready for the final synthesis in Lesson 12.
slo.safetyNotes: Swing the buzzer on a string in a clear space, with a string no longer than 1 m, a small light buzzer, and learners standing at least 3 m from the swinging path. The swinger wears eye protection if available and keeps the swing at a steady, gentle speed. Do not swing overhead. Keep the volume of videos moderate. Walk, do not run, during the walking demonstration. Keep bags and desks clear of the activity area.

LESSONS.overview: Learners revisit the three puzzles on the Driving Question Board and focus on Puzzle 2: why Baraka's horn sounds higher as the matatu approaches and lower as it moves away although he never changes it. After predicting, learners observe a YouTube demonstration of a moving sound source (ambulance/car horn passing), a classroom activity with a small buzzer swung on a string, and a Khan Academy explanation of the Doppler effect. They draw wavefronts for a moving source, link them to v = fλ from Lesson 6, and use f' = f v/(v - vs) and f' = f v/(v + vs) to calculate 418 Hz and 383 Hz for the matatu (35 Hz drop) and 744 Hz and 661 Hz for the ambulance. They add new questions to the DQB and complete Part B of the class model, noting that the same idea does not yet explain the fading radio, which belongs to Part C.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the matatu phenomenon: a horn that Baraka keeps at 400 Hz sounds higher as the matatu approaches and suddenly lower as it moves away (418 Hz then 383 Hz, observed in Lesson 1). Individually, in their notebooks, learners write a prediction answering: 'What is happening to the sound waves that makes the pitch change, when the horn itself does not change?' They draw a quick sketch of the waves in front of and behind the moving matatu. Then they discuss in pairs: 'If you were sitting inside the matatu, would you hear the horn change pitch? Why or why not?' and 'Would a stationary horn and a walking listener give the same effect?'
framework.teacherMoves: Display the DQB and point to Puzzle 2. Say: 'Baraka never touches the horn. It stays at 400 Hz the whole trip. Yet Wanjiru and Otieno hear 418 Hz coming and 383 Hz going. Something is changing, and it is not the horn.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after the question before anyone speaks. Circulate and note 3 common ideas (e.g. 'the horn gets louder so pitch rises', 'the matatu speeds up', 'the air pushes the sound'). Cold-call 4 learners to share predictions without judging: 'Thank you, Achieng. Who can add to or challenge that idea?' Record all predictions on the board under 'Our predictions'. Ask: 'Which prediction could we test today?' Separate loudness from pitch: 'Loudness is amplitude; pitch is related to frequency. Which one changed?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-and-sketch with Public Prediction Record: externalising initial ideas (including loudness-versus-pitch misconceptions) as sketches creates a shared baseline. Learners later compare their sketches with evidence, supporting conceptual change and ownership of the explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who confuse loudness with pitch; (2) learners who think the horn's frequency itself changes; (3) sketches that show waves squeezed together in front or stretched behind (a strong preconception). Tally on a clipboard how many of the 4 cold-called learners mention the motion of the matatu as the cause. Success indicator: at least half the class connects the pitch change to the matatu's motion, even without a mechanism.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather evidence in three parts. (1) Watch a short YouTube demonstration of a car or ambulance with a siren passing a stationary observer, listening for pitch on approach and recession, and a clip that shows wavefronts bunched ahead and spread behind. In a table they record: 'Moving toward me / passing / moving away' and the pitch heard (higher, same, lower). (2) Moving-buzzer activity in groups of 5: one learner swings a small buzzer on a 1 m string in a horizontal circle at steady speed in a clear space while 3 observers stand at different positions around the circle (about 3 m away) and one recorder notes whether the pitch is higher, lower or steady at each position. They repeat, then try a faster swing and note whether the difference becomes bigger. (3) Khan Academy: learners read or watch the Doppler effect section from 'Waves Applications (radio, radar, Doppler)' and note the two key formulas and what vs means. Learners then use the matatu data: with f = 400 Hz, v = 340 m/s, vs = 15 m/s, they calculate wavelength ahead of the matatu and behind it.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the video say: 'Do not just listen. Ask yourself: where is the sound higher, and where is it lower?' Play the clip twice: first for listening, second while pausing at 'approaching', 'passing' and 'receding' and asking for a show of hands for higher, same or lower. For the buzzer, demonstrate safe swinging first and state safety rules: 'Clear space, 3 metres back, gentle steady swing, no overhead swinging.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Where were you standing when the pitch was highest? What was the buzzer doing then?' After 10 minutes ask groups to report: 'Cold-call 3 groups: what did observers hear when the buzzer moved toward them? Away from them?' Prompt for the faster swing: 'What happened to the difference when the speed increased?' Introduce the Khan Academy materials: 'Find the two formulas and tell your partner what vs stands for.' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Draw wavefronts for a stationary horn (circles centred on the source) and then for a moving horn (circles whose centres shift forward), labelling compressed wavefronts ahead and stretched wavefronts behind.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Multi-source evidence gathering with a Data Table: combining video, hands-on modelling and an authoritative reading lets learners cross-check patterns (higher approaching, lower receding, bigger effect at higher speed). The physical model (the buzzer) makes the abstract wavefront model concrete, and the table organises observations for later explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each group's recorder correctly identifies higher pitch when the buzzer moves toward an observer and lower when it moves away. Check that learners notice the pitch is steady or neutral at the sideways position, and that the effect increases with speed. Ask 2 learners to explain in one sentence how the wavefront drawing shows compression ahead. Success indicators: correct table entries; consistent use of the word 'pitch' not 'loudness'; correct labelling of vs as the speed of the source.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build a causal explanation of the pitch change in three steps. Step 1 (conceptual): in pairs they use a wavefront diagram to explain that each wave crest is emitted from a position closer to the observer when the source approaches, so crests arrive closer together (shorter wavelength, higher frequency); behind the source crests are emitted from farther away, so they are spaced farther apart (longer wavelength, lower frequency). Step 2 (quantitative, linking to Lesson 6): the horn's true frequency is 400 Hz so the stationary wavelength is 340/400 = 0.85 m. In one period T = 1/400 s the matatu moves 15 m/s x (1/400) s = 0.0375 m. Ahead, the wavelength is 0.85 - 0.0375 = 0.8125 m so f' = v/λ' = 340/0.8125 = 418 Hz; the Doppler formula f' = f v/(v - vs) gives 400 x 340/325 = 418 Hz. Behind, λ' = 0.85 + 0.0375 = 0.8875 m so f' = 383 Hz; formula f' = f v/(v + vs) = 400 x 340/355 = 383 Hz. The drop is 418 - 383 = 35 Hz. Step 3 (practice): learners calculate the ambulance siren (700 Hz at 20 m/s): approaching 700 x 340/320 = 744 Hz; receding 700 x 340/360 = 661 Hz. They write a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph for Puzzle 2 and discuss: 'Why does the pitch change suddenly as the matatu passes, and why does it not change while it is parked?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Wavelength is the distance between crests. If the source chases its own waves, what happens to that distance?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to explain compression ahead and stretching behind. Model the wavefront diagram on the board step by step, then ask learners to complete the Step 2 working in pairs, circulating to check use of v = fλ from Lesson 6. Emphasise: 'The horn is always 400 Hz. The observer receives crests at a different rate.' Introduce the formulas and ask: 'Which formula is for approaching? Look at the denominator: v minus vs gives a smaller number, so the frequency is bigger.' Address misconceptions explicitly: 'The pitch change does not mean the horn changed, and it is not caused by loudness.' Ask learners to compute the ambulance values, then cold-call 4 learners for answers (744 Hz, 661 Hz) and ask: 'Why is the drop larger for the ambulance than for the matatu?' (higher speed and higher frequency). Ask learners to apply to Kenya: 'Where else do you notice this on Nairobi roads or on a train near Mombasa?' Finally, check a stationary-source, moving-observer extension only conceptually: 'If you walk toward a parked matatu, the crests reach you more often, so you also hear a higher pitch.' Do not go beyond the two source-moving formulas.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Mathematical Modelling: learners use the wavefront model to give a causal mechanism, then verify it quantitatively with v = fλ and the Doppler formulas. Calculating the same values already heard (418 Hz and 383 Hz) links the model to the real phenomenon and shows it has predictive power. Comparing matatu and ambulance numbers strengthens generalisation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners (1) correctly state that observed frequency, not source frequency, changes; (2) correctly select f v/(v - vs) for approach and f v/(v + vs) for recession; (3) arrive at 418 Hz, 383 Hz, 35 Hz, 744 Hz and 661 Hz; (4) rounded to the nearest Hz. Use a 2-question exit check on mini-whiteboards: 'Approaching or receding gives the higher pitch?' and 'What is the matatu's pitch drop?' Indicators of misunderstanding: using v + vs for approach, saying the horn changed, or confusing loudness with pitch. Re-teach with the wavefront drawing if more than a third of the class errs.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board. They (1) place a green sticky note on Puzzle 2 stating what they now know ('Horn stays 400 Hz; matatu approaching gives 418 Hz and receding 383 Hz because waves are squeezed ahead and stretched behind'), (2) mark Puzzle 1 (corner) and Puzzle 3 (fading radio) as answered or partly answered based on earlier lessons (diffraction, interference), and (3) write new questions on yellow notes, for example: 'Does the Doppler effect work for light or radio?', 'Why does the pitch change smoothly or suddenly?', 'How do police radar guns use this?', 'Could a faster matatu give a bigger drop?', 'Does the radio in the matatu also fade because of the Doppler effect?' They sort the questions into 'can answer now' and 'need more investigation'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to the DQB. Which of our questions did today's evidence answer? Which new questions did it raise?' Provide WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask 5 learners (cold-call) to read their sticky notes and justify where to place them. Prompt: 'Is the fading radio signal caused by the matatu's motion, or by the Ngong Hills reflecting the signal? What evidence do we have?' (linking to Lesson 9 interference, without re-teaching it). Highlight the question on higher speeds: 'Use the formula to predict: what would the matatu pitch be at 30 m/s?' as a take-home challenge. Group related questions (e.g. applications of Doppler: speed guns, ambulances, medical blood-flow) for Lesson 12. Praise precise wording and evidence-based reasoning.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a Tracking Tool: moving questions from 'unknown' to 'answered' and generating new ones makes progress visible and builds coherence across the unit. Sorting questions encourages learners to distinguish what current evidence can explain from what needs more investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes on Puzzle 2 include both mechanism (compression and stretching of waves) and numbers (418 Hz, 383 Hz). Check that new questions are testable and linked to the phenomenon. Success indicator: at least 5 new relevant questions, and at least 3 learners explicitly state that the radio fading is not due to the Doppler effect but to interference. Record learners who still confuse the two for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the single class model for the matatu mystery. Part A (corner/diffraction) and Part C (signal fading/interference) are reviewed from earlier lessons. The focus now is Part B (pitch/Doppler). In groups of 4 they draw a labelled diagram of the matatu moving at 15 m/s with wavefronts bunched ahead (wavelength about 0.81 m, observed pitch 418 Hz for Otieno standing ahead) and stretched behind (wavelength about 0.89 m, observed pitch 383 Hz for Wanjiru behind), with a note that the horn's true frequency stays 400 Hz and the stationary wavelength is 0.85 m. They write a short caption using the formulas f' = f v/(v - vs) and f' = f v/(v + vs) and add an ambulance inset (744 Hz approaching, 661 Hz receding). Each group adds a 'Still to explain' box noting that Part C needs a final check and that Lesson 12 will link all three parts.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the class model poster with Parts A, B and C. Say: 'Part B is blank. Using today's evidence, what must go in it?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then circulate and ask each group: 'Where is the pitch higher, and what is happening to the wavelength there? What stays the same?' Cold-call 3 groups to present, and ask the class to critique: 'Does this diagram explain why the pitch changes suddenly as the matatu passes? What evidence supports it?' Agree on one class version and fix it to the poster. Ask: 'Which parts of the model use v = fλ? Which use ideas from earlier lessons?' Point out connections: 'Part A used wavelength compared with the 4.0 m opening; Part B uses wavelength changing because the source moves; Part C uses overlapping waves. Different mechanisms, same wave ideas.' Conclude by assigning the summary table.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Peer Critique: learners revise a shared explanatory model using new evidence, and peer critique pushes them to justify each element. Linking three parts to the same phenomenon builds coherence and prepares for the final synthesis in Lesson 12.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a checklist: model shows compressed wavefronts ahead and stretched behind; labels 400 Hz source, 418 Hz and 383 Hz observed; states the formulas correctly; clearly says the horn does not change; separates the Doppler idea from diffraction and interference. Success indicator: at least 80 percent of groups include all five elements. Ask a final cold-call (3 learners): 'In one sentence, why does Wanjiru hear 383 Hz when the matatu drives away?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did learners clearly separate pitch (frequency) from loudness (amplitude), and did they accept that the horn's true frequency stays at 400 Hz? Which evidence (video, moving buzzer, or Khan Academy reading) most convinced them? Where did the wavefront diagram or the choice between v - vs and v + vs cause confusion, and did the 418 Hz and 383 Hz calculations make sense of what they observed in Lesson 1? Did any learners link the radio fading to the Doppler effect, and how well did they use earlier evidence on interference to correct this? What adjustments to the buzzer activity (speed, spacing of observers, safety) are needed? Which learners need additional support with substituting into the formulas, and how will the model be strengthened before Lesson 12?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the pitch of a moving horn or siren sounds higher when the source moves toward us and lower when it moves away, and that the effect is bigger for faster sources, even though the source itself does not change (matatu horn 400 Hz heard as 418 Hz and 383 Hz; ambulance 700 Hz heard as 744 Hz and 661 Hz).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency because of relative motion between source and observer: approaching f' = f v/(v - vs) and receding f' = f v/(v + vs), with v = 340 m/s for sound and wavelength and frequency linked by the wave equation v = fλ.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explained that Baraka's horn stays at 400 Hz, but the moving matatu (15 m/s) compresses the waves ahead of it so Otieno hears 418 Hz, and stretches them behind it so Wanjiru hears 383 Hz, a drop of 35 Hz. This completes Part B of our class model; the corner puzzle (Part A) and the fading radio (Part C) have different causes.
