LESSONS.title: Applications and Synthesis: FM, Ultrasound and the Final Explanation of the Matatu Phenomenon
LESSONS.aresKeywords: FM modulation, carrier wave, ultrasound, echo, diffraction, interference, Doppler effect, class model, final explanation, wavelength, frequency

slo.purpose: To apply wave properties to two technologies (FM radio and ultrasound imaging) and to combine evidence from Lessons 1 to 11 into one complete written and oral explanation of the matatu phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain that FM radio carries sound by changing the frequency of a 100 MHz carrier wave (a 1 kHz tone changes it by up to 75 kHz) while the amplitude stays constant. They calculate the 3.0 m wavelength of the 100 MHz carrier using the wave equation v = fλ. They explain that ultrasound imaging uses reflection and echo timing (as in sonar, Lesson 4) with 3.5 MHz waves travelling at 1540 m/s, giving a wavelength of 0.44 mm. They state the final explanation: the music is heard around the corner because sound wavelengths of 0.34 m to 1.7 m are comparable to the 4.0 m opening and diffract, while light of 5.0x10^-7 m hardly diffracts. The horn sounds 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding, although it stays at 400 Hz (Doppler effect). The FM signal fades about 1.5 m apart near the Ngong Hills because direct and reflected signals interfere destructively.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (revise the class model Parts A, B and C); constructing explanations (claim, evidence, reasoning); analysing and interpreting data (wavelength 0.85 m, ratio 0.21, 418 Hz, 383 Hz, 1.5 m); using mathematics (v = fλ, d = vt/2); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (oral and written presentation); asking questions (closing the DQB).
slo.attitudes: Appreciate how physics of waves is used in Kenyan communication and healthcare; show curiosity and intellectual honesty by revising earlier ideas with evidence; respect others' ideas during peer critique; take responsibility for group roles; show teamwork when presenting.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do waves behave when they meet obstacles or different media? 2. How are the properties of waves applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the culminating lesson. Learners apply wave properties to FM radio and ultrasound, compare their Lesson 1 model with the final class model (Parts A, B, C), close out the Driving Question Board, and deliver a complete written and oral explanation of how we hear a matatu around a corner we cannot see, why its pitch changes, and why its radio signal fades.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only low-volume sound sources in the classroom (buzzer, speakers at safe level; no loud horn). Keep cables and speakers off walkways. Ultrasound is shown by simulation or video only; no scanner is used on learners. Move chairs carefully during gallery walk and presentations. Keep the room open so everyone can hear peers speaking.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting how a radio can carry a voice on a 100 MHz wave and how a doctor can see a baby without cutting. They then observe two technology examples (FM modulation using a simulation or teacher demonstration, and an ultrasound imaging video/simulation) and use v = fλ and d = vt/2 to analyse them. In the Explain phase they use claim, evidence and reasoning to write a complete explanation of the matatu phenomenon, then rehearse and give an oral presentation. They close the DQB by sorting questions answered by evidence from Lessons 1 to 11, and finally compare the Lesson 1 initial model with the final class model (Part A corner/diffraction, Part B pitch/Doppler, Part C signal fading/interference). Mr Kamau, Wanjiru, Otieno and Baraka the matatu driver provide the continuing story.

framework.learnerExperience: Mr Kamau starts with the anchoring story: Baraka drives the Nairobi-Ngong route; the horn stays at 400 Hz and the radio at 100 MHz, yet Wanjiru and Otieno hear music around the corner, hear the pitch change, and the radio fades near the Ngong Hills. Learners individually write predictions in their notebooks for two new questions: (1) The FM station sends a voice on a 100 MHz wave. How could a wave of that frequency carry a 1 kHz voice or music? (2) A clinic in Kisumu uses sound with a frequency far above what we can hear to see a baby inside the mother. How could sound make a picture? Learners also draw a quick sketch with one sentence for each prediction, then share with a partner using a 'turn and talk' for 2 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Today we use everything we have learned in eleven lessons. Before we learn anything new, I want your own ideas.' Display the two questions. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence after each question before learners write. Circulate and note 3 different ideas, for example 'radio sends sound through air directly' or 'echo helps the picture'. Cold-call 4 learners: 'Wanjiru's seat, tell us what you think the 100 MHz wave does with the voice.' Ask: 'Which earlier lesson might help us with the baby scan? Think about Lake Victoria fishers.' Record 3 predictions on the board without judging. Say: 'We will test these by the end of the lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with prior-knowledge activation: learners commit to an idea before evidence. Linking ultrasound to the Lesson 4 echo and sonar idea and the radio to the 100 MHz station in the phenomenon helps learners notice that their predictions are built from earlier evidence, so later comparison of predicted and observed ideas shows how their thinking changed.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for a written prediction plus a reason for both questions. Indicators: learner mentions echo, reflection or sonar when predicting about ultrasound; learner mentions 'changing' something about the radio wave when predicting about FM. Note how many of 4 cold-called learners connect to an earlier lesson. Tally common misconceptions (for example 'the voice is the radio wave') for use in Explain.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 with roles (recorder, speaker, calculator, materials manager). Station 1, FM modulation: using the PhET Sound simulation or the teacher's graphs, plus the Khan Academy Waves Applications resource (radio, radar, Doppler), they observe that the carrier is 100 MHz and a 1 kHz audio tone changes the carrier frequency by up to 75 kHz while the amplitude stays constant. They calculate the carrier wavelength using the wave equation v = fλ: λ = 3.0x10^8 / 1.0x10^8 = 3.0 m. They sketch a carrier whose waves bunch closer and spread farther apart following the tone. Station 2, ultrasound: they watch a short ultrasound imaging video and use the wave equation to find the wavelength of 3.5 MHz waves in soft tissue travelling at 1540 m/s: λ = 1540 / 3.5x10^6 = 4.4x10^-4 m = 0.44 mm. They explain that pulses reflect from boundaries between tissues and the echo time gives depth using d = vt/2, just as in sonar on Lake Victoria (30 m depth). Station 3, evidence revisit: using their notebooks and class charts, they list the strongest evidence from Lessons 4, 8, 9 and 11 (0.85 m wavelength, 4.0 m opening, ratio 0.21, 1.5 m fading spacing, 418 Hz and 383 Hz). Groups rotate every 8 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are scientists collecting evidence for the final explanation. Record numbers with units.' At Station 1, ask: 'The audio tone is 1 kHz. Is it the 1 kHz that travels through the air as the radio wave? What changes in the carrier, and what stays the same?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Clarify: the carrier is 100 MHz = 1.0x10^8 Hz and its frequency changes by up to 75 kHz; the amplitude is constant. At Station 2, ask: 'Why is a wavelength of 0.44 mm useful for seeing small details?' and 'How is this like the Lake Victoria fisher's sonar?' Prompt: 'If an echo returns from a boundary, what do we need to know to find its depth?' Circulate with a checklist; correct unit errors (Hz vs MHz) on the spot. Do not re-teach diffraction or Doppler; point back: 'Remember Lesson 11: what did we find for the horn?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data analysis with multiple representations (simulation graph, sketch, calculation, video): learners meet the same wave ideas in three forms, which strengthens understanding that FM and ultrasound rely on the same properties of waves (frequency, wavelength, speed, reflection) studied in earlier lessons. The station rotation gives repeated chances to connect each technology back to the matatu phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (a) calculate 3.0 m for the FM carrier wavelength and 0.44 mm for ultrasound with correct units; (b) state that FM changes the carrier frequency while the amplitude stays constant; (c) use d = vt/2 correctly in the ultrasound explanation. Use a 3-item exit slip at each station: 'What changes in FM? What reflects in ultrasound? Which number would you use for depth?' Aim for at least 80% of groups with correct answers; reteach at the next station if fewer.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build the Final Explanation using a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) frame, one section per puzzle. Part A (corner): Claim: sound is heard around the building because it diffracts. Evidence: sound wavelengths are 0.34 m to 1.7 m (0.85 m for 400 Hz) compared with the 4.0 m opening, ratio 0.21; light is 5.0x10^-7 m, so the ratio is about 1.3x10^-7. Reasoning: diffraction is greatest when wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap, so sound bends and light does not. Part B (pitch): Claim: the horn sounds 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding although it stays at 400 Hz. Evidence: f' = 400x340/(340-15) = 418 Hz and f' = 400x340/(340+15) = 383 Hz, a 35 Hz drop. Reasoning: the moving source compresses waves ahead and stretches them behind (Doppler effect). Part C (fading): Claim: the FM signal fades near the Ngong Hills because direct and reflected signals interfere. Evidence: 100 MHz gives λ = 3.0 m; weak spots are half a wavelength apart, 1.5 m. Reasoning: destructive interference where path difference = (n+1/2)λ, constructive between them; the station never changes. Learners add a closing paragraph linking one technology (FM modulation or ultrasound) to the properties used. Then each group rehearses a 2-minute oral presentation and groups present to the class, with listeners using a checklist.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A good explanation uses a claim, numbers as evidence, and the physics rule as reasoning. Do not just tell the story; explain why.' Provide the CER frame on the board. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds for individual thinking before groups write each section. Circulate and ask: 'Which number proves your claim? Which lesson gave you that rule?' and 'Why does light not bend round the corner while sound does? Use the ratio.' Cold-call 5 learners to read one reasoning sentence aloud and ask 2 others to add a missing piece. Listen for common errors: confusing amplitude with pitch, saying the horn really changes frequency, saying the station weakens. Correct: 'Does Baraka change the horn? Does the station change?' For presentations, assign each group one part to lead and ask the audience to give 'two stars and a wish' using the checklist. Allow about 2 minutes per group with 1 minute of questions. Use respectful language and make sure every member speaks.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with oral argumentation: writing and speaking require learners to connect each claim to measured data and a wave rule. Explaining aloud and receiving peer questions exposes gaps and builds a coherent causal story across diffraction, Doppler and interference, rather than three separate facts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a rubric with 4 criteria: (1) all three claims correct; (2) uses exact figures (0.85 m, 4.0 m, 418 Hz, 383 Hz, 3.0 m, 1.5 m); (3) reasoning names diffraction, Doppler effect and destructive interference correctly; (4) clear oral delivery. Look for evidence that the learner states that the horn stays at 400 Hz and the station never changes. Collect written explanations to mark after the lesson. Target: at least 75% of learners score 3 of 4 or above; note learners needing support for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board created in Lesson 1: 'How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?' In groups, they take their own sticky-note questions from the board and sort them into three columns: Answered (with evidence and the lesson number), Partly answered, and New questions. For each Answered question they write the evidence in one sentence (for example, 'Why does the torch beam stop but music not? Lesson 8: ratio 0.21 against 1.3x10^-7'). They add at least one new question linked to the key inquiry about applications (for example, 'How does the phone network use waves like FM does?' or 'Why does a hospital choose 3.5 MHz?'). They identify the two KICD key inquiry questions and place their notes under them.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board started as a wall of puzzles. Let's see which ones we can now answer, and with what evidence.' Give each group 5 minutes. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which question was hardest to answer and why?' Cold-call 4 groups to read one answered question and its evidence. Challenge: 'Which question can you answer only partly? What more would you need to measure?' Ask: 'Which question shows the waves behaving at obstacles, and which shows waves being applied in daily life?' Record new questions on a separate 'Next Steps' chart. Affirm learners whose questions have changed from 'what happened?' to 'why does it happen?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record of learning: sorting questions by the evidence that answers them makes progress visible and shows learners that science questions are answered gradually from several investigations. New questions model how science continues and connects the lesson to the key inquiry questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group sorted at least 80% of its questions with a lesson number and an evidence sentence. Indicators: learner cites a number (for example 0.21, 418 Hz, 1.5 m) rather than just saying 'we learned it'; at least one new question per group that is testable or linked to a technology. Note questions that remain unanswered and record them for the teacher reflection.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners place the Lesson 1 initial model beside the current class model. Working in the same groups, they finalise the three-part class model on a large chart. Part A (corner/diffraction): a plan view of the building and the 4.0 m opening, with wavefronts of sound (0.85 m) spreading around the corner and a straight, blocked light beam (5.0x10^-7 m). Part B (pitch/Doppler): the matatu moving at 15 m/s with wavefronts bunched ahead (418 Hz) and stretched behind (383 Hz), with the horn labelled 400 Hz at the source. Part C (signal fading/interference): direct and reflected 100 MHz signals from the Ngong Hills with wavelength 3.0 m and fading spots 1.5 m apart. Learners add a small 'applications' box showing FM modulation (carrier 100 MHz, 1 kHz tone, 75 kHz deviation) and ultrasound (3.5 MHz, 1540 m/s, 0.44 mm). They then complete a comparison table: 'What we thought in Lesson 1', 'What we know now', 'Evidence that changed our mind'. Groups do a gallery walk, leave one comment for each other group, and revise their own model after feedback.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is useful if it predicts and explains. Check that every arrow, label and number matches evidence.' Display the Lesson 1 model beside the new one. Ask: 'What did we draw in Lesson 1 for the corner? What does our model now include that was missing?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups answer. Cold-call 4 groups to name one change and its evidence. During the gallery walk, give each learner 2 sticky notes: one 'strong because' and one 'what about...?' Ask: 'Can your model predict what happens to the corner if the horn were 1000 Hz? What would the wavelength be?' (0.34 m, bends less than 200 Hz at 1.7 m, using Lesson 8). Ask: 'If the matatu drove at the same speed away from you, would the horn change again?' Close by asking each group to state in one sentence the main idea of the unit. Collect charts and the comparison tables.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision and comparison (L1 vs final): placing the first and final models side by side shows the change in thinking and ensures that evidence drives revision. Peer feedback during the gallery walk tests whether the model explains all three puzzles with one connected set of wave properties.
framework.formativeAssessment: Checklist for each model: Part A includes the 4.0 m opening, 0.85 m wavelength and the light comparison; Part B includes 400 Hz, 418 Hz, 383 Hz and the compression/stretching idea; Part C includes 3.0 m, 1.5 m and the direct plus reflected signals; applications box includes FM and ultrasound figures correctly. In the comparison table, look for at least 3 specific changes backed by evidence. Observe whether learners accept and use peer feedback to revise. Record learners who can predict the effect of changing a variable (such as pitch or source speed).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners connected FM modulation and ultrasound to earlier lessons (Lesson 4 echo and sonar, Lesson 6 v = fλ) without prompting? Did any learners still think the horn really changes frequency, the radio station weakens near the Ngong Hills, or that the voice itself travels as the 100 MHz wave? Which part of the final explanation (A, B or C) needed the most support, and which pieces of evidence were most convincing to learners? Were oral presentations balanced so that quieter learners such as those who rarely spoke earlier also contributed? Which DQB questions remained unanswered and could become starting points for the next unit? Consider whether the timing of the station rotation allowed enough time for the written explanation and what to adjust next time.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that music is heard around the building but the torch beam is blocked; the matatu horn sounds 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding; the FM radio fades near the Ngong Hills about every 1.5 m; the FM carrier is 100 MHz and changes frequency with a 1 kHz tone (up to 75 kHz) while amplitude stays constant; ultrasound of 3.5 MHz in soft tissue at 1540 m/s has a wavelength of 0.44 mm and its echoes make an image.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that sound waves of wavelength 0.34 m to 1.7 m are comparable to the 4.0 m opening and diffract, while light of 5.0x10^-7 m hardly does; that the Doppler effect changes the frequency heard when a source moves; that interference of direct and reflected signals makes weak and strong spots; and that FM radio and ultrasound imaging apply frequency, wavelength, reflection and the wave equation v = fλ.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The music is heard around the corner because sound diffracts around the 4.0 m opening (0.85 m wavelength, ratio 0.21) but light does not. The horn really stays at 400 Hz; it sounds 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding because the moving matatu compresses waves ahead and stretches them behind (Doppler effect). The FM signal fades near the Ngong Hills because the direct and reflected 3.0 m waves interfere destructively about 1.5 m apart, while the station never changes.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Physics Grade 10: Properties of Waves (Sub-strand 2.1) Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Today you will write your Final Explanation of the matatu phenomenon. Think about Baraka's matatu on the Nairobi-Ngong route, and about Wanjiru and Otieno standing around the corner of a building on a busy Nairobi street. Baraka keeps his horn at 400 Hz and his radio on one 100 MHz FM station. Use the wave equation v = fλ and the figures from our lessons: sound in air travels at 340 m/s, light in air travels at 3.0x10^8 m/s, the street opening is 4.0 m wide, and the matatu moves at a constant 15 m/s. Write your answer in the space under each prompt. For every explanation, give a claim, the evidence (with numbers and units) and your reasoning. Show your working for every calculation. Use the words pitch for frequency and loudness for amplitude. Refer back to the Driving Question Board and your class model (Parts A, B and C) where it helps.

sections.title: Part A: Why the music turns the corner but the torch beam does not
sections.prompt: Wanjiru and Otieno cannot see the matatu behind the concrete wall, but they hear its music clearly. A torch beam from the matatu would be blocked. (a) Use v = fλ with 340 m/s to calculate the wavelength of the horn (400 Hz) and the wavelengths of the lowest (200 Hz) and highest (1000 Hz) notes of the music. (b) Calculate the ratio of the horn wavelength to the 4.0 m opening, and the approximate ratio for visible light of wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m. (c) Write a claim-evidence-reasoning explanation of why the music is heard around the corner and the torch beam is not. (d) Which would be heard better around the corner, a 200 Hz note or a 1000 Hz note? Explain.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Horn: λ = v/f = 340/400 = 0.85 m. Lowest music note: 340/200 = 1.7 m. Highest music note: 340/1000 = 0.34 m. So the music has wavelengths from 0.34 m to 1.7 m.
(b) Horn ratio = 0.85/4.0 = 0.21. Light ratio = 5.0x10^-7/4.0 = about 1.3x10^-7.
(c) Claim: The music is heard around the corner because sound waves diffract (bend) around the 4.0 m opening, but light hardly diffracts at all, so the torch beam is blocked. Evidence: sound wavelengths of 0.34 m to 1.7 m (the horn is 0.85 m, ratio 0.21) are comparable to the 4.0 m opening, while light of wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m has a ratio of about 1.3x10^-7. In the ripple tank, narrow gaps made waves spread out, and in the classroom corner demonstration the tone was heard but the torch beam did not reach us. Reasoning: diffraction is the spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap, and it is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. Sound meets this condition so it spreads round the corner. Light's wavelength is far smaller than the gap, so it travels almost in a straight line (rectilinear propagation) and the wall casts a shadow.
(d) The 200 Hz note (λ = 1.7 m) would be heard better. Its longer wavelength is closer to the 4.0 m opening than the 0.34 m wavelength of the 1000 Hz note, so it diffracts more. Higher pitches bend less than low pitches.

sections.title: Part B: Why the horn changes pitch
sections.prompt: Baraka drives past at a constant 15 m/s and never changes his horn, which has a true frequency of 400 Hz. (a) Use f' = f v/(v - vs) and f' = f v/(v + vs) with v = 340 m/s to calculate the frequency Otieno hears as the matatu approaches and the frequency Wanjiru hears as it moves away. Round to the nearest Hz. (b) Find the drop in pitch. (c) Explain, using wavefronts, why the pitch heard changes although the horn stays the same. (d) Which fixed quantity stays the same at the horn itself?
sections.exemplar:
(a) Approaching: f' = 400 x 340/(340 - 15) = 400 x 340/325 = 418 Hz. Receding: f' = 400 x 340/(340 + 15) = 400 x 340/355 = 383 Hz.
(b) Drop = 418 - 383 = 35 Hz.
(c) This is the Doppler effect, an apparent change in frequency caused by relative motion between source and observer. The horn keeps producing 400 waves every second. As the matatu moves forward, each wavefront is sent out from a point closer to the listener ahead, so the wavefronts are compressed, the wavelength is shorter and more waves arrive each second, giving a higher pitch (418 Hz). Behind the matatu, each wavefront is sent from a point further away, so the waves are stretched, the wavelength is longer and fewer arrive each second, giving a lower pitch (383 Hz). The speed of sound stays 340 m/s, and v = fλ links the changed wavelength to the changed frequency heard.
(d) The horn's own frequency stays at 400 Hz; Baraka never changes it. Only the frequency received by the listener changes.

sections.title: Part C: Why the FM radio fades near the Ngong Hills
sections.prompt: The matatu radio is tuned to one 100 MHz FM station that never changes, yet it fades and crackles at certain spots near the Ngong Hills and comes back a few metres later. (a) Use v = fλ with 3.0x10^8 m/s to find the wavelength of the signal. (b) Explain, using the words superposition, path difference and interference, why the signal fades at some spots and is strong between them. (c) How far apart are the weak spots, and how does this follow from your answer to (a)? (d) In the classroom, two speakers both played 340 Hz. Give the wavelength and say whether a path difference of 1.00 m or 0.50 m gave the quiet spot. How does this support your explanation in (b)?
sections.exemplar:
(a) λ = v/f = 3.0x10^8/1.0x10^8 = 3.0 m.
(b) Near the Ngong Hills the radio receives two signals: one directly from the transmitter and one reflected from the hillside. The two waves overlap and add together (superposition). Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths (nλ) the waves reinforce, which is constructive interference, and the signal is strong. Where the path difference is (n + 1/2)λ the waves cancel, which is destructive interference, and the signal is weak and crackles. Moving the matatu a short distance changes the path difference, so the radio fades and then returns even though the station never changes.
(c) Weak spots are half a wavelength apart, so 3.0/2 = 1.5 m apart.
(d) For 340 Hz, λ = 340/340 = 1.00 m. A path difference of 0.50 m (half a wavelength) gave the quiet spot, and 1.00 m gave a loud spot. The quiet spots disappeared when one speaker was covered because there was then no second wave to cancel the first. This shows that the same interference idea explains the fading FM signal, only with a wavelength of 3.0 m instead of 1.00 m.

sections.title: Part D: Using wave ideas in technology
sections.prompt: Wave properties are applied in everyday life. (a) Fishers on Lake Victoria use sonar. A pulse returns after 0.040 s and sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. Calculate the depth and explain why you divide by 2. (b) A doctor uses ultrasound of frequency 3.5 MHz, which travels at 1540 m/s in soft tissue. Calculate its wavelength in millimetres and state how the image is formed. (c) In FM radio, a 1 kHz tone is sent on a 100 MHz carrier. State what changes in the carrier and what stays constant.
sections.exemplar:
(a) d = vt/2 = 1500 x 0.040/2 = 30 m. The pulse travels down to the lake bed and back up to the boat, so the total distance covered is twice the depth; dividing by 2 gives the depth.
(b) λ = v/f = 1540/3.5x10^6 = 4.4x10^-4 m = 0.44 mm. The ultrasound pulses reflect from boundaries between different tissues, and the echoes returning (timed using d = vt/2) are used to build an image without cutting.
(c) In FM, the frequency of the 100 MHz carrier changes in step with the 1 kHz tone (by up to 75 kHz), while the amplitude stays constant.

sections.title: Part E: Putting it all together
sections.prompt: Write a complete explanation for the Driving Question: How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves? Your answer must have three paragraphs matching Parts A, B and C of the class model. In each paragraph give a claim, evidence with numbers from this assessment, and reasoning. Then say how your final model differs from your first model in Lesson 1.
sections.exemplar:
Part A (corner): The music is heard around the building because sound diffracts. The sound wavelengths of 0.34 m to 1.7 m (the horn is 0.85 m, ratio 0.21 to the 4.0 m opening) are comparable to the opening, and diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. Light of wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m has a ratio of about 1.3x10^-7, so it hardly bends and the torch beam is blocked by the wall.
Part B (pitch): The horn really stays at 400 Hz. Because the matatu moves at 15 m/s, it compresses the waves ahead of it, so Otieno hears 418 Hz, and stretches them behind it, so Wanjiru hears 383 Hz, a drop of 35 Hz. This is the Doppler effect, caused by relative motion between source and listener.
Part C (fading): The 100 MHz FM signal has wavelength 3.0 m. Near the Ngong Hills the direct signal and the signal reflected from the hillside interfere. They cancel (destructive interference, path difference (n + 1/2)λ) at weak spots about 1.5 m apart and reinforce between them, so the radio fades and returns although the station never changes.
Change from the first model: In Lesson 1 I only had guesses and knew a wave is a disturbance that carries energy. My final model gives three separate causes (diffraction, the Doppler effect and interference), each supported by evidence and calculation using v = fλ.

rubric.criterion: Explaining diffraction at the corner (Part A)
rubric.excellent: Correctly calculates all wavelengths and ratios (0.85 m, 1.7 m, 0.34 m, 0.21, about 1.3x10^-7) and gives a full claim-evidence-reasoning explanation linking wavelength to gap size, including why low pitches bend more than high pitches.
rubric.proficient: Calculates most wavelengths and ratios correctly and explains that sound bends and light does not because of wavelength compared with the opening, with small gaps in reasoning.
rubric.developing: States that sound bends and light does not but gives little or no use of wavelength compared with the 4.0 m gap, or has calculation errors.

rubric.excellent: Uses both Doppler formulas correctly to get 418 Hz, 383 Hz and a 35 Hz drop, and clearly explains compressed and stretched wavefronts while the horn stays at 400 Hz.
rubric.proficient: Gets the correct frequencies and gives a mostly correct explanation of higher and lower pitch with some vagueness about wavefronts.
rubric.developing: Gives incorrect values or says the horn itself changes, or does not link pitch change to motion.

rubric.excellent: Finds λ = 3.0 m, uses path difference (nλ and (n+1/2)λ) correctly, links to the 1.5 m spacing, and connects it to the 340 Hz speaker results.
rubric.proficient: Finds the wavelength and explains destructive and constructive interference of direct and reflected signals, with minor errors in path difference or spacing.
rubric.developing: Mentions weak signal without explaining the overlap of direct and reflected waves, or gives an incorrect wavelength.

rubric.criterion: Calculations and application to technology (Part D)
rubric.excellent: Correctly calculates 30 m, 0.44 mm and describes FM modulation, with units and explanations of d = vt/2.
rubric.proficient: Gets most calculations correct with units and a basic description of reflection and modulation.
rubric.developing: Calculation errors, missing units, or does not explain the division by 2.

rubric.excellent: Uses claim, evidence and reasoning in every part, uses correct terms and units, uses Kenyan context, and compares the final model with the Lesson 1 model.
rubric.proficient: Mostly uses claim, evidence and reasoning with correct terms and units, with some weak links between parts.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we hear a matatu around a corner that we cannot see, and why does its pitch change and its radio signal fade as it moves?

lessons.title: The Matatu Mystery: Launching the Phenomenon
lessons.observed: Write what you observed about the three puzzles: the music heard around the corner while the torch beam was blocked by the wall, the matatu horn (true frequency 400 Hz) heard at 418 Hz while approaching and 383 Hz while receding at 15 m/s, and the 100 MHz FM radio fading at certain spots near the Ngong Hills though the station never changes.
lessons.learned: Write what you learned today: a wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter (as shown by the slinky pulse and the sound from the matatu horn), and good scientific questions are testable.
lessons.explained: Write what you can explain so far, and what you cannot yet explain: give your best first idea for each of Parts A (corner), B (pitch) and C (fading signal) in your model, and list one question from the Driving Question Board that you want answered next.

lessons.title: Waves Travel in Straight Lines: Rays, Wavefronts and the Blocked Torch Beam
lessons.observed: In the ripple tank at 10 Hz in deep water we saw straight, evenly spaced plane wavefronts with wavelength 3.0 cm, and we calculated v = 0.30 m/s. A torch beam through a slit travelled in a straight line, and a block in its path made a dark shadow with a sharp edge.
lessons.learned: In a uniform medium waves travel in straight lines (rectilinear propagation). A wavefront joins points in phase, and a ray is drawn at 90 degrees to the wavefronts to show direction. Light travels at 3.0x10^8 m/s in air and obeys this rule.
lessons.explained: We can explain why a torch beam from the matatu is blocked by the concrete wall: the light rays travel straight and cannot pass through or around the wall, so a shadow forms where Wanjiru and Otieno stand. We cannot yet explain why the music is heard around the corner, and that question stays on the Driving Question Board.

lessons.title: Bouncing Back: Reflection and the Laws of Reflection
lessons.observed: We observed ripples (10 Hz, wavelength 3.0 cm) bouncing off a barrier, light rays bouncing off a plane mirror with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, and an echo returning after 0.50 s from a wall 85 m away.
lessons.learned: Waves reflect from surfaces according to the law of reflection: the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r, measured from the normal, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. Reflection does not change the frequency, wavelength or speed of the wave in the same medium. An echo is a reflected sound wave.
lessons.explained: Sound from the matatu can reach Wanjiru and Otieno by reflecting from walls, and the Ngong Hills can reflect the FM radio signal, giving a second signal that will later be used to explain the fading spots. Reflection alone does not yet explain how sound bends around the corner (Part A), why the pitch changes (Part B), or why the signal fades (Part C), so we need more evidence in later lessons.

lessons.title: Echoes, Sonar and Hall Design: Putting Reflection to Work
lessons.observed: We observed that a clap 85 m from a wall returns as an echo after 0.50 s, that a closer wall gives a delay too short to hear separately, and that a Lake Victoria sonar pulse returned after 0.040 s.
lessons.learned: We learned that sound reflects from hard surfaces following the law of reflection, that d = vt/2 because the sound travels there and back, that a separate echo needs at least 17 m in air, and that hard and soft surfaces change how a hall sounds.
lessons.explained: We can explain that the sonar depth is 1500 x 0.040 / 2 = 30 m and that reflection can send some matatu sound along the street, but reflection alone does not explain why sound reaches people around the 4.0 m opening, why the horn pitch changes, or why the FM signal fades.

lessons.title: Refraction: Speed and Direction Change
lessons.observed: In the ripple tank, waves moved from deep water (v = 0.30 m/s, wavelength 3.0 cm) into shallow water (v = 0.20 m/s, wavelength 2.0 cm) at 10 Hz, and the wavefronts bunched closer and the direction turned toward the normal. In the PhET simulation a light ray in air at 40 degrees entered water and bent to about 29 degrees, toward the normal; going from water to air it bent away.
lessons.learned: Refraction is a change of direction of a wave caused by a change of wave speed at a boundary. A wave that slows down bends toward the normal; a wave that speeds up bends away from the normal. The frequency stays the same while the speed and wavelength change.
lessons.explained: Refraction describes how waves behave when they enter a new medium or depth, but it does not explain why the matatu music is heard around the building, because the sound stays in the same air. We still need other ideas to explain the corner, the pitch change and the fading radio signal near the Ngong Hills.

lessons.title: Refraction Calculations and the Bent Straw: Why Wavelength Changes but Frequency Does Not
lessons.observed: In the ripple tank at 10 Hz, the waves had a wavelength of 3.0 cm in deep water and 2.0 cm in shallow water and bent at the boundary. A ray of light entering water at 40 degrees bent to about 29 degrees from the normal. A straw in water looked broken at the surface.
lessons.learned: When a wave is refracted, its frequency stays the same because the source sets it, while its speed and wavelength change (v = fλ). The refractive index n = sin i / sin r = c/v; for water n = 1.33 and light travels at 2.26x10^8 m/s. Wavelength depends on the speed of the wave and the frequency of the source.
lessons.explained: The straw looks bent because light from its underwater part bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, and our eyes trace the rays back in straight lines to a shallower apparent position. The straw itself is straight. This does not yet explain why sound turns the corner, but we now have the tool v = fλ to work out wavelengths, such as 0.85 m for the matatu horn at 400 Hz, which we will use in Lessons 7 and 8.

lessons.title: Diffraction: Gap Size and Wavelength
lessons.observed: In the ripple tank at 10 Hz (λ = 3.0 cm), waves passing through a wide gap of 12 cm mostly travelled straight, while waves passing through a narrow gap of 3 cm or 1.5 cm spread out in almost circular wavefronts. The PhET simulation showed the same pattern when slit width or wavelength was changed. The street opening around the building is 4.0 m wide.
lessons.learned: Diffraction is the spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap. It is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap, and is very small when the wavelength is much smaller than the gap. The wavelength can be found from v = fλ, for example 0.30 ÷ 10 = 0.03 m = 3.0 cm.
lessons.explained: This partly explains Part A of the matatu puzzle: waves can bend around the corner if their wavelength is comparable to the 4.0 m opening. We still need to compare the wavelengths of sound and light with 4.0 m in Lesson 8 to explain why the music is heard around the corner but the torch beam is blocked.

lessons.title: Diffraction and the Corner Puzzle: Why Sound Turns the Corner but Light Does Not
lessons.observed: We observed that a low tone (about 200 Hz) was heard more clearly than a high tone (about 1000 Hz) around the corner of the partition, while the torch beam did not reach us. We calculated that the matatu horn (400 Hz) has wavelength 0.85 m, the music ranges from 1.7 m (200 Hz) to 0.34 m (1000 Hz), and light has wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m, compared with the 4.0 m street opening.
lessons.learned: We learned that diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to or bigger than the gap. For the horn, the ratio of wavelength to gap is 0.85/4.0 = 0.21, so the sound clearly bends, while for light the ratio is about 1.3x10^-7, so it hardly bends at all. Lower pitches (longer wavelengths) bend around the corner more than higher pitches.
lessons.explained: Wanjiru and Otieno hear the matatu music around the building because the sound waves of wavelength 0.34 m to 1.7 m are comparable to the 4.0 m opening and diffract around the corner, while the torch beam, with wavelength 5.0x10^-7 m, hardly diffracts and is blocked by the wall. The pitch change and the fading radio signal are still open questions on our Driving Question Board.

lessons.title: Interference and the Fading Radio: Loud Spots, Quiet Spots and Weak FM Signal
lessons.observed: In the ripple tank, two sources made bands of strong ripples and calm water. With two speakers playing 340 Hz we found loud and quiet spots in the room, and the quiet spots vanished when one speaker was covered.
lessons.learned: Overlapping waves add together (superposition). When the path difference is nλ the waves reinforce (constructive interference, loud or strong). When it is (n+1/2)λ they cancel (destructive interference, quiet or weak). For 340 Hz, λ = 1.00 m, so a path difference of 1.00 m gives a loud spot and 0.50 m gives a quiet spot.
lessons.explained: Near the Ngong Hills, the 100 MHz FM signal has λ = 3.0 m. The direct signal and the signal reflected from the hillside overlap and cancel at weak spots about 1.5 m apart, then reinforce between them. The radio fades and returns even though the station never changes.

lessons.title: Standing Waves and Musical Notes: Guitar Strings, Nodes and the Half-Wavelength Link
lessons.observed: We observed that a slinky and a guitar string of length 0.65 m, when shaken or plucked, showed fixed points of no movement (nodes) and points of large movement (antinodes). The fundamental pattern had 2 nodes and 1 antinode; the second pattern had 3 nodes and 2 antinodes. A shorter string (0.325 m) and a tighter string gave a higher note.
lessons.learned: We learned that a standing wave forms when a wave and its reflection travel in opposite directions and superpose. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, and for the fundamental L = λ/2. With v = 143 m/s on a 0.65 m string, λ = 1.30 m and f = 110 Hz; the second harmonic is 220 Hz, and a 0.325 m string also gives 220 Hz. Length and tension set the note.
lessons.explained: We explained that the weak FM spots near the Ngong Hills are about 1.5 m apart because the direct and reflected signals overlap, and the 100 MHz signal has wavelength 3.0 m, so weak spots are half a wavelength (1.5 m) apart, just as nodes on a string are λ/2 apart. This strengthens Part C of our model, while the pitch change of the matatu horn (Part B) still needs explaining.

lessons.title: The Doppler Effect: Why the Matatu Horn Changes Pitch
lessons.observed: We observed that the pitch of a moving horn or siren sounds higher when the source moves toward us and lower when it moves away, and that the effect is bigger for faster sources, even though the source itself does not change (matatu horn 400 Hz heard as 418 Hz and 383 Hz; ambulance 700 Hz heard as 744 Hz and 661 Hz).
lessons.learned: We learned that the Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency because of relative motion between source and observer: approaching f' = f v/(v - vs) and receding f' = f v/(v + vs), with v = 340 m/s for sound and wavelength and frequency linked by the wave equation v = fλ.
lessons.explained: We explained that Baraka's horn stays at 400 Hz, but the moving matatu (15 m/s) compresses the waves ahead of it so Otieno hears 418 Hz, and stretches them behind it so Wanjiru hears 383 Hz, a drop of 35 Hz. This completes Part B of our class model; the corner puzzle (Part A) and the fading radio (Part C) have different causes.

lessons.title: Applications and Synthesis: FM, Ultrasound and the Final Explanation of the Matatu Phenomenon
lessons.observed: We observed that music is heard around the building but the torch beam is blocked; the matatu horn sounds 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding; the FM radio fades near the Ngong Hills about every 1.5 m; the FM carrier is 100 MHz and changes frequency with a 1 kHz tone (up to 75 kHz) while amplitude stays constant; ultrasound of 3.5 MHz in soft tissue at 1540 m/s has a wavelength of 0.44 mm and its echoes make an image.
lessons.learned: We learned that sound waves of wavelength 0.34 m to 1.7 m are comparable to the 4.0 m opening and diffract, while light of 5.0x10^-7 m hardly does; that the Doppler effect changes the frequency heard when a source moves; that interference of direct and reflected signals makes weak and strong spots; and that FM radio and ultrasound imaging apply frequency, wavelength, reflection and the wave equation v = fλ.
lessons.explained: The music is heard around the corner because sound diffracts around the 4.0 m opening (0.85 m wavelength, ratio 0.21) but light does not. The horn really stays at 400 Hz; it sounds 418 Hz approaching and 383 Hz receding because the moving matatu compresses waves ahead and stretches them behind (Doppler effect). The FM signal fades near the Ngong Hills because the direct and reflected 3.0 m waves interfere destructively about 1.5 m apart, while the station never changes.
